subtopic: INFLATION-REASON FOR SPECIFIC PROPOSALS TO LABOUR CONCERNING INFLATION BUT NOT UNEMPLOYMENT
INFLATION-REASON FOR SPECIFIC PROPOSALS TO LABOUR CONCERNING INFLATION BUT NOT UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, since according to the expert opinion of many there is now a turn-around taking place in the North American continent with the problem of inflation diminishing in comparison with the problem of unemployment, which most people expect to increase, and this is supported by most recent indicators, will the minister inform the House why the proposals that were sent to organized labour and provincial governments contained certain specific targets for the reduction of inflation, which is not likely to be the increasing problem, but contained no specific targets or other suggestions, and not even an intimation of them in respect of the reduction in unemployment levels?

speakeroldname: Hon. John N. Turner (Minister of Finance):
subtopic: INFLATION-REASON FOR SPECIFIC PROPOSALS TO LABOUR CONCERNING INFLATION BUT NOT UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am just suggesting to the hon. member that a large number of working papers have been circulated, but I am not going to sustain or base my position on any alleged working paper that may have been published by the media. What I am saying to him is that inflation and unemployment are equally difficult problems for this country to face and unless we can solve the problem of inflation, unemployment will become worse in terms of the stimulus injected into the North American, particularly American, economy. Inflation remains a recurring problem in terms of our competitive position with the United States and other major competitors and the disadvantage we will incur and are incurring in terms of our costs will become very dangerous for this country in the next 12 to 20 months unless we do something about it now.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. Has the decision of the National Energy Board to reduce the export tax on Canadian crude by 80 cents any implications for the government's policy with respect to the export of crude oil at the rate of 680,000 barrels a day in mid-summer? In other words, was the reduction made because of the decline in markets there or has there been some fundamental change in our decision regarding the amount of oil we want to export?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: OIL-REASON FOR REDUCTION IN EXPORT TAX-EFFECT OF DECLINE IN EXPORTS ON EQUALIZATION OF DOMESTIC PRICE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the target we set for 1975 was 800,000 barrels a day. In fact, the level has been much lower, around 650,000, and indeed in the last several months it has been in the neighbourhood of 500,000 barrels a day. The decision to lower prices was made partly because of the representations received from western Canada and partly because of the desire to maintain the exports at a certain level. That was the basis for dropping the price, to meet the competition in the U.S. There has been no fundamental change in the maximum levels we had in mind.

subtopic: OIL-REASON FOR REDUCTION IN EXPORT TAX-EFFECT OF DECLINE IN EXPORTS ON EQUALIZATION OF DOMESTIC PRICE
speechtext:
As I understand it, basically the answer is a softening in the market rather than a change in policy.

subtopic: OIL-REASON FOR REDUCTION IN EXPORT TAX-EFFECT OF DECLINE IN EXPORTS ON EQUALIZATION OF DOMESTIC PRICE

The over-all level of exports being somewhat lower has meant a greater exposure for the treasury, than was the case when the export tax was at a higher level.

subtopic: OIL-REASON FOR REDUCTION IN EXPORT TAX-EFFECT OF DECLINE IN EXPORTS ON EQUALIZATION OF DOMESTIC PRICE

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs. In light of the statement issued by the minister today regarding the important conference at Geneva to review the provisions on the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons, will the Canadian government, in addition to the proposals and policies outlined in the statement, give consideration to putting forward to the conference a proposal that the signatories of the treaty, including Canada, agree not to sell nuclear reactors or other materials capable of being diverted from peaceful purposes for the creation of materials for nuclear weapons to any country which is not a party to the non-proliferation agreement and which does not accept the safeguards prescribed by the International Atomic Energy Agency?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gerard Pelletier (Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs):
subtopic: CONFERENCE ON TREATY ON NON-PROLIFERATION OF NUCLEAR WEAPONS-SUGGESTED AGREEMENT NOT TO SELL REACTORS TO NON-SIGNATORY COUNTRIES

Subject to these limitations, the approximate average weekly cost of training per trainee by fiscal year is as follows: 1967-68, $28.28; 1968-69, $33.10; 1969-70, $33.52; 1970-71, $35.09; 1971-72, $46.80; 1972-73, $58.13; 1973-74, $64.60; 1974-75, $58.44. It should further be noted that these figures do not include the costs of training allowances, for which full-time trainees may be eligible.

The House resumed, from Monday, May 5, consideration of the motion of Mr. Lang that Bill C-41, respecting the stabilization of net proceeds from the production and sale of western grain and to amend certain statutes in consequence thereof, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Agriculture; and the amendment thereto of Mr. Baker (Grenville-Carleton) (p. 5468).

subsubtopic: PROCEEDS FROM THE PRODUCTION AND SALE OF WESTERN GRAIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate last evening on the amendment to Bill C-41, I mentioned a number of things. First of all, I suppose I should state clearly that the amendment is asking for a referral of the subject matter to committee without the bill being dealt with in principle. If there is one time in my 17 years of political debating in the House of Commons that I wish the government would adhere to the wishes of the opposition, this is the occasion. I am not given to begging very often, but if it would do the trick I would beg the government to comply with the amendment now before the House.
I intend to deal, within the next 30 minutes or so allotted to me in this debate, with my reasons for this request. But first let me say that something very interest-

May 6, 1975
Western Grain Stabilization
ing happened last evening. The hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil) was speaking about inventory and the difficulty of equating just what inventory really deals with. The minister in charge of the bill, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang), interrupted the hon. member and asked him this question which is to be found at page 5495 of Hansard:
I wonder whether the hon. member can tell me how he develops the fear that any bin measuring is required-
The minister then asked: "Where is the inventory?" and the hon. member for Moose Jaw replied: "I would assume the inventory is in the farmer's bins." To which the minister replied: "Nonsense".
The minister is piloting the bill through the House and we must deal with the legislation that is before us. At page 11 of the bill, subclause (4) of clause 9, paragraph (A) refers to "the opening inventory, in bushels, of farm stocks of such grain". How do you find a farmer's stock of such grain, Madam Speaker? You measure it in bins most of the time. At least, I hope most farmers keep their grain in bins. The paragraph continues, "for the year under review, determined as being,the closing inventory". Paragraph (B) refers to the "closing inventory, in bushels, of farm stocks of such grain determined in December of the year under review".
I do not know whether the hon. member for Moose Jaw is interpreting that particular clause correctly, but I do not know how else to interpret it. When the minister who is piloting this bill through the House says that the equating of inventory in bins is sheer nonsense, one can realize why we on this side of the House would like the whole subject matter of the bill dealing with grain income stabilization sent to the agricultural committee so the committee can hear briefs from farmers and farm organizations.
The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Goodale) said in his speech that all farm organizations agree with the bill, that all farm organizations think it is a necessary piece of legislation. He said the same thing of Bill C-19. As reported at page 26 of issue No. 4 of the agriculture committee's proceedings of November 7, 1974, the hon. member said:
It is interesting to look at what the farm reaction has been in fact. According to the announcements and pronouncements of the various farm groups with respect to this two-price wheat program ... every farm group that I have heard of endorsed it. At the moment I cannot think of an exception that voiced a contrary opinion last fall to this legislation.
That is what the hon. member said about Bill C-19, Madam Speaker. I have with me quotations from all the farm briefs, and if time allows I should like to read them. Every farm group that appeared before the committee, including even the Palliser Wheat Growers which the hon. member for Assiniboia brought down here, wanted changes made in the bill. The National Farmers Union wanted changes made, so did the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, Unifarm of Alberta and the Ontario Wheat Growers. So it is only logical that we cannot take the word of the hon. member for Assiniboia in regard to Bill C-41.
To emphasize the conflict of jurisdiction in the field of agriculture, this very afternoon the agriculture committee is sitting. Members of the opposition have stated that this grain income stabilization bill is very complex and confusing and that members of parliament knowledgeable of

agriculture should be here, either explaining it to those who do not understand it or listening to the explanations of the experts on the government side who are proposing the legislation. But the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) said, "To heck; that's not even agriculture. The agriculture committee sits". So it is sitting. It is with regret that I have to point that out to the House, because I have always believed that as grain income goes, so goes agriculture for the whole of Canada.
Last night I was saying that the Minister of Justice has not done anything beneficial for Canadian wheat farmers during the whole of his political career. The only major piece of legislation that he ever got through parliament was an enlargement, to take into account the costs of production and inflation, of a piece of legislation put forward formerly by the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) when he was prime minister at the time the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) was minister of agriculture-namely, the cash advances legislation. What else has the minister done? He brought forward this bill about four years ago. Last night I stated that defeat of the bill four years ago saved the farmers a great deal of money. I went to the trouble of looking up exactly how much money was saved, Madam Speaker. I found that in the crop year 1970-71, under the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act, $39 million was paid out. In the crop year 1971-72, under the same act, $86,135,000 was paid out.
The defeat of the grain income stabilization bill four years ago carried a price tag: the cancellation of the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act, the cancellation of PFAA and the cancellation of the government's right or ability to pick up the barley deficits. Those three measures were cancelled in lieu of this grain income bill. Yet in those two crop years alone, over $100 million was paid out through the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act. In the crop year 1972-73, $2,918,000 was paid out under the same act and the money went into the Wheat Board pool account. In the crop year 1973-74, $5,832,000 was paid out into the Wheat Board pool account. So somewhere in the neighbourhood of $129 million has been paid out under the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act. In other words, members of parliament who contributed to the defeat of the grain income stabilization bill saved the farmers $129 million on that basis alone.
That is only one aspect. Another relates to payments under PFAA. In the year 1971, nearly $5 million was paid out to the farmers under PFAA. If we had passed the grain incomes stabilization bill four years ago, that money would never have gone out. In 1972, the amount was $5.4 million, and in 1973 it was $524,000. I have not done the mathematics-I could, because the figures are here before me-but this amounts to about $11 million that would not have been paid out to the farmers had this House of Commons passed the grain incomes stabilization bill of four years ago.
There is another matter involved, and that is deficiencies in the barley pool account for the years 1970-71 and 1971-72. If this House had passed the old grain stabilization bill, the government would not have had to pick up those deficiencies. In 1970-71, the barley pool account lost
May 6, 1975

$9,945,000, and in 1971-72 it lost $3 million. If parliament had passed that bill, the government would not have picked up those losses or paid out those amounts, so in effect parliament saved the farmers millions of dollars which this minister tried to take away from them, and would have if we had readily passed that bill.
The reason I am making this case is to show beyond a shadow of doubt that the complexities of Bill C-41 are not understood by members of this House, so the subject matter should be referred to the committee. Let us take a look at operation LIFT, that other great measure the Minister of Agriculture sometimes likes to boast about while most people realize that it was a colossal error. The minister says this had to be done. I heard him recently in Saskatchewan say that it was just one of those necessary things. He said that world wheat production had to be contained back in 1969. What are the facts? Farmers cut down their wheat acreage at the direct order of the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board. I say it was a direct order, but that is a polite term; it was as a result of browbeating and blackmail by the minister in charge of the Wheat Board.
Let me give the House some figures from the 1973-74 annual report of the Canadian Wheat Board. The total acreage in wheat in 1969 was 24,400,000, and in 1970 this had dropped to 12 million acres. That was a reduction of over 12 million acres as a direct result of the order of the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board. What happened in the rest of the world in respect of wheat production? Reading from page 3 of the same annual report, we find that world production of wheat back in 1969-70 reached about 10 billion bushels. Production has increased successively each year since, until in 1973-74 world wheat production reached 13.6 billion bushels. In causing the Canadian farmer to reduce the production of wheat by reducing the number of acres, the minister effectively lost markets and sales at higher prices for Canadians. This cost the farmers quite a bit.
Wheat seeded in 1970 would have sold in 1971, 1972 and possibly in 1973. The price to the farmer at that time varied from $2.15 a bushel to a low of $1.60 a bushel. According to this report, the 12 million acres yielded an average of 26 bushels to the acre. Anybody with a pocket computer can figure out what that reduction in Canadian wheat cost the Canadian farmer. The equation is 26 times 12 million times about $2 a bushel. That is colossal amount of money which this minister cost the Canadian farmer. Let me be specific by saying that it was a direct loss to the farmers of Saskatchewan, the very people the minister attempts to represent sometimes in this House.
The most soul-saving thing I can say as a member of parliament representing farmers in my constituency is that I cannot be blamed because the minister did not bring into operation the LIFT program in my area. I was not asked to recommend it to parliament or to vote for it. I was not asked to say whether it was good or bad. At the time I did say it was bad. There were newspaper headlines to the effect that as a result of the LIFT operation some $60 million would be paid out to the farmers. I remember headlines two inches high in the Globe and Mail at that time. The money paid out under the LIFT program was closer to $64 million. I have given the equation regarding
Western Grain Stabilization
how much was lost, and it appears to me that about $600 million was lost of the prairie farmers.
Is it any wonder that with that kind of track record we on this side ask the minister not to bring forward this complex bill and ask us to vote yea or nay on it? Please do not ask us whether we fully understand clause 11 which gives a calculation on the aggregate amount of stabilization payments. We want it worked out. It is not good enough that we understand it; the farmers must understand it. When there is a crop failure the farmers will, without a shadow of doubt, come to their member of parliament and ask why they are not getting some of this money. They will tell us they paid 2 per cent on last year's crop and the government contributed 4 per cent, so they expect to get something out of the fund. We will have to convince those farmers that clause 11 is being interpreted correctly by the officials-and that will not be an easy task.
The farmers have to understand this bill, and they do not understand it today. I suggest that no farm organization today understands either clause 10 or clause 11. In fact, the minister last evening proved beyond a shadow of doubt that, rather then the hon. member for Moose Jaw not having read the bill, the minister has not read it. The minister has to go on his past record in respect of the old stabilization bill. He gave us an equation, in his speech, in relation to his old grain stabilization bill of four years ago. I think I proved beyond doubt that the old bill should have been defeated. Perhaps this one is an improvement. The old bill referred to gross sales, as this one does, although from time to time when reading it I have noted some reference to net income.
I am not suggesting I fully understand the bill, and I am not ashamed to admit that I do not fully understand it. I have a rough idea how it is going to work. However, it is not surprising that farmers in western Canada do not understand it. One of the biggest jokes you can tell farmers at a meeting in western Canada is that whenever the government suggests they should do something, if they do the very opposite they will come out better. That joke goes over well with the farmers because this minister has proved it to be accurate.

The minister suggests that they laugh, but do not do it. I suggest that if they work out the equation I gave which shows that the minister cost the farmers some $600 million as a result of his LIFT operation, they will realize that if they do not do the very opposite of what he tells them to do, then they should. There is no question about that in my mind. The minister says they do not do it. Let me quote from the February edition of the Country Guide, a well known publication, one of the better ones. This magazine does not go off half-cocked in respect of its editorials. Generally speaking, research is carried out: the editors of the magazine research articles which they write, having in mind the betterment of agriculture in Canada. This is what appears in the editorial section. The heading reads, "Don't go 'All out'". This has reference to the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Justice telling the farmers to grow all the wheat they can this year. The editorial reads:

May 6, 1975
Western Grain Stabilization
Spring isn't far way. The time's approaching when farmers will make final decisions on what crops and what acreages they're going to seed this year.
Since last fall, there's been plenty of advice on that second point. It's mostly come from the mouths of politicians; it revolves mostly around one central message: "Grow everything you can. Canada and the world rely on the heroic efforts of you farmers to keep us from starvation".
That is what the politicians have been telling the farmers. The minister says that the farmers listen to him. This magazine, which publishes and researches articles on western and Canadian agriculture in general, does not quite agree. The article ends saying:
This is not the year to sacrifice the future, or take abnormal risks in order to grow extra grain. At least not unless there's something more concrete than politicians' promises at the end of the road.
It states pretty clearly that the farmers should not buy the promises of politicians but should look for something better. It is as though the farmers listen to the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board and then proceed to do the very opposite. The request by the opposition to refer the subject matter of this bill to the agricultural committee or another committee of the House of Commons bears very careful consideration by the government for another reason. A committee which has before it a piece of legislation can amend its clauses. I should know, because I have moved amendments on a number of occasions. However, if one should amend, say, subclause (b) of a clause, this would affect subclauses (a), (c) or (d). But if the subject matter were referred to committee and the committee heard witnesses, then the legal minds of the Department of Justice and the Department of Agriculture could draw up a bill which would comprise roughly what the farmers and the farm organizations want. This makes much more sense than the proposals of some members of parliament who may have great legal backgrounds.
It is difficult to amend a bill that is already drafted, in order to meet the very divergent views which may exist in the farming community. Prior to this amendment being moved, I stated my opinion that the bill is not regional enough. That question could be dealt with. I have asked myself how we can amend Bill C-41 and equate several regions within the Canadian Wheat Board area. I have looked at this bill and tried to figure out how it could be amended so there would be 14 different regions within the prairie area. I could not figure out a clause which would have that effect. If the subject matter were referred to the committee, a bill could be drafted to deal with the geographic areas which naturally exist on the prairies. The area of the Wheat Board extends from Manitoba to the interior of British Columbia. The Peace River area is a natural geographic area. The inner lake region of Manitoba is another natural geographic area, as is the area around the Carrot River in the Mackenzie District. None of these areas is the same as the Regina plains area.
This bill is not regional enough. Therefore, many farmers feel they could have a crop failure and would not be able to obtain a payment. This bill also deals specifically with the question of sales. Sales depend upon the volume sold and the price. If twice as much is sold at half the price, the total sale is the same as if you had sold half as much. Therefore, it is not good enough to deal strictly with

sales. We saw in Canada, during the last 365 days, the west coast tied up for 206 days. This greatly affected sales. In a study entitled "Transportation Implications of Canada's Trade with Japan" by Keith A. J. Hay and S. R. Hill, we find this statement:
This strike, along with a strike by lakes crews, which totally eliminated water movement from Thunder Bay, continued into the next crop year. Bottlenecks have been particularly severe upon westward movement of prairie grain. The Wheat Board estimated that about $350 million of wheat sales were lost in 1974 as a result of transportation difficulties in the west, and countless potential sales were jeopardized with the decline in the Canadian reputation for reliability.
I wanted to put that specifically on the record because this bill deals with sales. Sales can be affected by conditions which have nothing to do with the farmer. The farmer can grow the wheat and pay his costs in respect of fuel, production, machinery and taxes. The Lord, I suppose, can interfere with his crop and instead of bringing rain can bring hail. However, the farmer has other problems with which he must deal which are far beyond his control, such as the problem of moving his grain through the normal pipeline to the markets. We have seen these problems this year.
We have also seen this Minister of Justice interfere directly with collective bargaining. Last May 8 he directly interfered with collective bargaining by telling the unions they were right and the company was wrong. Therefore, he prohibited meaningful negotiations taking place in a two-month period between May 8 and July 8. He deliberately cost the farmers $350 million which the Canadian Wheat Board says it lost in the calendar year 1974. So, is it any wonder that members of parliament become pretty leery about anything this minister touches with regard to agriculture?
The minister was born on a farm, but he left the farm because he hated agriculture. I say to you, Madam Speaker, and to all members of this House of Commons, that he still hates agriculture. He has done nothing for agriculture in western Canada. Every piece of legislation in which he has been involved, with the exception of the cash advances legislation, has cost western Canada money. Every time he turns around he costs western Canada money. The greatest thing the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau) could do would be to leave him strictly with justice or some other department. While I do not advocate that the Canadian Wheat Board be placed in the hands of the Minister of Agriculture, I do say: Give me Whelan or anybody other than this minister who has cost the farmers money with respect to every piece of legislation he has attempted to pilot through this House.
The minister of agriculture for the province of Saskatchewan says that we should not rush this bill. All the prairie ministers say that we should look at it because it is not fully understood. All the amendment says is that we should study the subject matter and then determine what we really want. If the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Justice are prepared to put in 4 per cent of the gross sales in the form of government money, the farmers can use that money. Since we do not particularly trust the track record of the minister and the government, this makes sense to me.
May 6, 1975

Normally, legislation before the House must be dealt with in a hurry because of the need for change. Labour unions must tell their men to go back to work, so parliament has to deal with it; corporate rip-offs take place, so parliament has to deal with them. This is a long-term measure, in the minister's own words. Since only four or five payments will be made in the next 20 years, why tie the farmer that length of time to a piece of legislation which demands that he pay in 2 per cent of the sales without giving him some warning in this complicated bill? No payments will be made in 1975 or 1976 because probably sales will be good and prices may hold up. Payments will be made when the bill has been in effect for a number of years.
Then there is the question of compulsion in the bill. In clause 5 it is stated that by 1978 the farmer must make up his mind whether he wants to opt in or out of the program. I say that if the minister is not careful, farmers will not understand the bill and will not know whether to exercise the option. However, if the committee travels across Canada, studying the subject matter of the bill and discussing it with farmers, farmers will have a better basis for understanding it and they will know whether they prefer to opt in or out of the program and run their own insurance scheme.
For all these reasons, I believe that the amendment before us is justified and in conclusion I should like to plead with members of the House to pay heed to it and vote accordingly.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise again to take part in this debate because I have some additional reasons to put forward for the subject matter of the bill being referred to the standing committee. It is my strong conviction that if that were to happen, as a result of the proceedings of the standing committee and what its members would hear, the minister and parliament would wish to make substantial changes to the legislation before it was brought back to the House. I also want to present the views of one of the provinces which will be affected by this legislation, views that the province is presenting today in Ottawa.
One reason that I think the subject matter of the bill should be referred to the standing committee is that I think members of the committee, farmers and farm organizations in the Wheat Board area, must realize that what the bill does in one area of the western grain industry is to shore up and insure operations on the open market. I know that what I will now say will not be supported by the Conservatives or, for that matter, by the Liberal and Social Credit parties, but it is my opinion and that of my party that this legislation should be applied in such a manner so as not to benefit those who are selling grain on the open market: I must protest this bill being used to shoreup the Winnipeg commodity exchange. If any farmer is foolish enough to sell his feed wheat, oats and barley on the open market and wants to take his chances with the fluctuating, open market prices, I see no reason whatsoever why we should use federal legislation to stabilize income which is obtained on the open market rather than
Western Grain Stabilization
through the orderly marketing system of the Canadian Wheat Board.
So far as I am concerned, if the farmer wishes to become involved with grain speculators, then he should damn well take his chances and forfeit his opportunity to receive any payments from the grain income stabilization plan. The payments should go to those who deliver wheat to the Canadian Wheat Board. The government should licence feed lots and feed mills as agents of the Canadian Wheat Board, so that farmers who deliver directly to a feed lot or a feed mill would be eligible to participate in a proper grain income stabilization plan. As is obvious from the bill, that matter has not been considered by individual farmers and farm organizations.
The major difficulty with the legislation before us is the fact that those who do the best in terms of income, collect the most whenever there is a pay-out. Surely that flies in the face of any principles of a good insurance or stabilization program. One has only to look at any unemployment insurance, health insurance or a host of other programs: this provision in the bill flies in the face of the principles underlying any such program.
In 1970-71, and again in the past few weeks, the New Democratic Party proposed that any grain stabilization program should be integrated and meshed with crop insurance programs. This is the best, easiest, simplest and most understandable manner in which to operate. The two fit logically together. I would point out that with the repeal of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act which was a form of crop insurance-everyone out west called it the "dry bonus" that worked reasonably well and although it was not all-inclusive in the risks it covered, at least it was a beginning, the federal government, to its credit and it is to be commended for it, increased its contributions to the crop insurance programs to cover 50 per cent of the premiums under crop insurance in all provinces. The rate of participation in crop insurance was 66 per cent of farmers in Manitoba and 62 per cent in Saskatchewan. I suspect it was somewhere in the same neighbourhood in Alberta. Each year, thousands of additional farmers come under it and I predict that in another year or two the plan will be almost universal.
When we have that amount of participation, the program will become that much better because under it we will be able to provide greater coverage and greater benefits when crop losses occur. It is logical and proper for an income stabilization plan to be integrated and meshed with a crop insurance program. Crop insurance covers the risks that Mother Nature sometimes inflicts on farmers. Income stabilization will cover economic risks such as the world situation and other conditions over which the farmer has no control.
I agree that the government should be commended for being prepared to put up $50 million or $60 million a year-it might be more than that in some years-out of the national treasury, from all the people of Canada, toward stabilizing the incomes of western grain producers. We all support that idea. But the content of this legislation makes a farce of any proper grain income stabilization program. It completely betrays the principle of a real grain income stabilization program.
5516

May 6, 1975
Western Grain Stabilization
I think the government did a deplorable thing when it repealed the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. When it increased its contribution to the crop insurance program it deserved commendation. But there was some $8 million to $10 million left in the old PFAA fund. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) does not want to put that into crop insurance. That is what it was raised for. Levies were imposed on farmers and they contributed to the PFAA fund. It was to help them in the way of pay-outs when they suffered crop losses due to weather conditions and natural hazards. That is what the crop insurance program does now. I would like to know why the minister will not put the money left over from the PFAA fund into the crop insurance program, where it rightfully belongs.
What does the minister want to do? He wants to start his grain income stabilization fund with that money. That money belongs to the crop insurance fund and not to the minister to do with as he pleases. This matter needs to be considered in committee; it is part of the subject matter of the legislation before this House. Even though I have commended the government for its intention to put up $50 million or $60 million per year toward a grain income stabilization program, I want to remind the House that it will not be additional money from Canadian taxpayers; it is money the government had already saved when it succeeded in disposing of the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act. When that legislation was in operation, the Government of Canada paid anywhere from $20 million to $65 million per year as its share of the cost of grain storage in the terminals of Canada. That was a good principle: it should have applied to all grains, not just wheat. But the notion as a whole was to contribute toward the cost of a national inventory or national pantry-storage for the world's hungry.
The burden of those storage costs was not borne by farmers alone; the nation as a whole contributed. For the last two successive crop years the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang), through the Canadian Wheat Board, has not had to pay a nickel toward the cost of grain storage. The federal government has saved somewhere between $40 million and $120 million just in two crop years. The government plans through this legislation to give out with one hand money it has already taken away with the other hand. I think it is a disgrace that the government no longer participates in a meaningful way in the sharing of grain storage costs from coast to coast, not just in western Canada. This is a national inventory or pantry which is maintained for our customers, for the aid programs we have and for the needy and hungry of the world.
That kind of program should be reinstated, instead of the minister saying that the government is prepared to pay up to $40 million toward grain storage. The problem is that I am afraid he plans to pay up to $40 million toward grain storage but also to hand out grants, loans and whatnot to private enterprise commodity exchange types who want to put up inland terminals which will cost farmers more and will destroy hundreds of communities in the prairie provinces which can and should be viable. These communities are composed of two, three or four generations of people who have put in a lifetime of endeavour.

When I was listening to the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) the other day, he said that the old grain stabilization bill of 1970-71 was withdrawn by the government because it was compulsory. He was talking about the participation in the plan proposed under the bill before us. I want to remind the hon. member that that is not why the bill was withdrawn. It was withdrawn because the opposition parties in parliament were unanimous in their opposition to the way it was structured and to the way it was intended to be implemented. Every farm organization was opposed to it, all three western provinces were opposed, and the Minister of Justice was stubborn and refused to listen. It required a court case, involving four farmers taking the government and the then minister of finance to court and applying for a writ of mandamus to force the minister of finance to pay $92 million owing to the Canadian Wheat Board by the federal government. That is what forced the withdrawal of that bill, and thank goodness it happened.
While I admit that the minister has made some improvements in this legislation over the old legislation, it still flies in the face of the principles of a good grain income stabilization plan. It may be called a bill guaranteeing incomes, or whatever expression comes to mind. I notice the Minister of Justice has left the chamber, but I see the hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley (Mr. Mclsaac) is here and I want to put on record the position of the province of Manitoba. I should tell the hon. member that Manitoba is presenting its position right now to the Standing Committee on Agriculture. I expect he will receive a copy of this tomorrow, or perhaps I can make one available to him tonight. I want to put on the record Manitoba's position as follows:
Manitoba Crop Insurance Corporation and the Government of Manitoba are very concerned over the proposed Prairie Grain Stabilization Act as set out in Bill C-41. While we commend the Government of Canada for its intention to provide a greater degree of stability for the prairie grain producers, we have serious reservations with regard to the type of stabilization program that is being proposed.
We said earlier that the objective of crop insurance is to provide farmers with a means to protect themselves against serious financial losses caused by acts of nature.
One would assume that the objective of the grain stabilization plan would be to provide farmers with a means to protect themselves against serious financial losses caused by economic events beyond their control. Indeed, Bill C-41 is being portrayed as having that purpose.
We regret to say that if that were the objective of the proposed Prairie Grain Stabilization Act, it could not be achieved by the measures envisaged in Bill C-41. What is more serious in our view, however, is the fact that Bill C-41 does not have as its specific purpose the protection of farmers against losses due to economic events beyond their control. One of the most exasperating aspects of the bill is that it is next to impossible to detect the rationale behind it, and this lack of rationale together with the extreme complexity of the bill makes any attempt at explaining this important legislation to farmers an exercise in frustration.
Yet, since the scheme proposed in Bill C-41 is a contributory plan, farmers should know what insurance they are buying; in other words, the plan must relate to the needs of individuals, and it should be possible for individuals to determine what benefits would accrue to them if the events against which they are insuring themselves should occur. That is a cardinal principle of all insurance plans, be they private, mixed private and social such as crop insurance, or universal social insurance schemes such as workers' compensation, unemployment insurance, hospital or health insurance.
May 6, 1975

A second cardinal principle of all such schemes is that indemnities are paid to those who experience the ill effects of the event against which the plan provides insurance, and not to others. The proposed Prairie Grain Stabilization Act sins against both these principles; in fact it completely ignores them.
For example, a farmer who insures his crop with Manitoba Crop Insurance Corporation knows what he insures himself for; he knows to what level he will be indemnified if his yield is below the insured level. A worker who pays unemployment insurance knows what he may expect in benefits in the event he loses his job and fails to find another. That is as it should be. In contrast, a person participating in the proposed Prairie Grain Stabilization Act has no way of knowing when he will receive benefits, how much he will receive, or whether he will receive benefits when he really needs them.
Secondly, Manitoba Crop Insurance Corporation will indemnify only those insured farmers who suffered specified losses but will make no payments to all insured farmers because the over-all yield in the province was below the five-year average. Similarly, the Unemployment Insurance Commission will pay benefits to insured persons who lose their job, but will not make payments to all those making unemployment insurance contributions on the basis that there is a slack in the economy. Yet that is precisely what the measures proposed in Bill C-41 purport to do.
In a nutshell, payments will be made by the grain stabilization fund if the proceeds from the sale of a proportion of the prairie grain crop in any year falls below the average proceeds in the previous five-year period, after adjustments have been made for changes in certain-but by no means all-expenses incurred in production. Participating farmers will receive payments proportionate to their contributions. Whether individual farmers actually suffered declines in receipts or income is immaterial under that plan.
If Manitoba Crop Insurance Corporation operated on that principle it could conceivably have taken the $8.2 million paid in indemnities in 1974 and distributed them to insured farmers on the basis of their premium contributions. It is quite possible that farmers with very high yields would have received large payments and farmers with a total crop loss would have received far less.
I am sure the hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Mackasey) will be interested in what comes next:
If the Unemployment Insurance Commission operated on the same principle as the grain stabilization plan, it would calculate for all of Canada the average annual bill for wages and salaries on which unemployment insurance contributions are made, adjust it for changes in the number of unemployment insurance contributors and for certain changes in the consumer price index, and if the adjusted total wage bill fell below the average of the previous five years, the Unemployment Insurance Commission would make a payment to all wage and salary earners. Each would be paid proportionate to this contributions; those who had paid the maximum would receive most; those who had paid less would receive less, and the unemployed who had made little or no contributions would receive little or nothing. We doubt whether such a scheme to "stabilize the net proceeds from wages and salaries in Canada" would meet with the approval of the Canadian people. Yet this is precisely the method "to stabilize the net proceeds from the production and sale of western grain" that has been presented as Bill C-41 to the Parliament of Canada for approval.
Earlier in our submission we commended the Government of Canada for its intention to provide a degree of stability for the prairie grain producers. We are appreciative of the willingness of the federal government to ask the Canadian people to set aside some $50 million or $60 million per year-perhaps more-to be channelled to prairie grain producers if at some future date economic factors beyond their control cause a severe decline in receipts from the sale of prairie grains. While we appreciate the intent, and while we approve of the establishment of a prairie grain stabilization fund, we respectfully suggest that a more rational, more equitable and more effective plan should be adopted than the one proposed in Bill C-41.
Now we come to the meat of the argument presented by Manitoba, and to their proposal. Indeed, this is what we proposed in 1970-71 but the minister refused to listen. I
Western Grain Stabilization
mentioned it again last Tuesday night. The Manitoba brief continues:
We suggest that the present all-risk crop insurance programs operative in the western provinces could be broadened to include price guarantees. Prices for the various crops could be adjusted from year to year to reflect changes in the cost of production and to protect profit margins so that net farm incomes would be kept commensurate with the general standard of living in Canada. By adding price guarantees to the present yield and quality guarantees of the crop insurance program, farmers could be offered a complete package of basic income protection.
The program could be operated by the crop insurance administration presently existing in the western provinces. With a slight addition to staff, Manitoba Crop Insurance Corporation could administer a much more equitable crop and income insurance program than is envisaged in Bill C-41. It would also make it unnecessary to establish a complete, new administrative organization to administer a separate western grain stabilization program.
Above all, the approach suggested by Manitoba Crop Insurance Corporation is consistent with the cardinal principles of mixed private and social insurance, that the insured knows what he is insured against and what his benefits will be, and that payments are not made at random but to those who need them.
Madam Speaker, if that does not tell us that the subject matter of this bill should be referred to the Standing Committee on Agriculture, I do not know what does. If you were to apply the principle of this bill to unemployment insurance or any other social program, the people just would not stand for it. It provides for making payouts to those who get the most-the ones who get the most, get the most; and the ones who get the least, get the least. If that is stabilization of income, I'm a monkey's uncle!
The subject matter of this bill flies in the face of its title and flies in the face of the principle of income stabilization. Surely a simpler and more equitable system would be to guarantee prices. A member of a crop insurance board told me that if they were to administer crop insurance and income stabilization together, all they would have to do is add one column on the crop insurance form. I am not an overly suspicious fellow, Madam Speaker, and I would not want to accuse the government of any political designs on western Canada, so I will give them the benefit of the doubt and accept their intentions as being good. I commend them for trying to stabilize grain incomes.
In the dirty thirties we on the prairies had a bitter experience with the organization of the relief inspectors and the separate, little, private administrative machines. I do not know why the Minister of Justice needs a separate, massive administrative machine to implement a grain income stabilization plan when the machinery is already in place. All four western provinces have viable, functioning crop insurance programs. To its credit, the federal government pays half the premiums but the provinces administer the programs and bear that cost. As well, the farmers contribute to the program.
This is what should be done when grain incomes suffer as a result of things other than natural hazards. If the world market crashes or other economic disasters over which the farmers have no control take place, at that point the crop insurance administration-let us call it a crop incomes insurance plan-should step in. This would be a step in the direction of a real incomes policy in Canada. This is what farmers and farm organizations want to talk about, and they could do so if the subject matter of the bill were referred to the standing committee.
29S61-6'/2

Western Grain Stabilization
This bill is a real mare's nest. I had a couple of good lawyers look it over and they are still scratching their heads. If anything would cause farmers to lose confidence and withdraw their support from any proposal for grain income stabilization, this is it. That is why we ask that the subject matter be referred to the standing committee. The way the minister wants to apply this legislation flies in the face of the principle of grain income stabilization or any kind of income insurance and opposes the title of the bill. As the Government of Manitoba has said, it would be an exercise in frustration to try to deal with this legislation as it stands. To have farmers ask questions and give information would be a complete waste of time if the legislation were to pass in its present form, because within one or two crop years the majority of grain farmers in western Canada would be so fed up and angry that they would start opting out of the plan. They would realize they had been had again; that this is not an effective way to deal with the wildly fluctuating incomes of grain farmers.
All parties in this House agree we must do something; that never again must the grain industry be afflicted by the wild variations of income which it has experienced in the last 40 years. Although we agree, surely this is not the way to do it. The legislation must be as simple as possible. I submit, on behalf of my party, that the simplest and most practical way of doing it would be to guarantee prices and bring in adjustments related to costs of production so that the incomes of farmers are comparable with the incomes of the other people of Canada. It is as simple as that. The government's payment of $50 million, $60 million or $80 million a year will cover half or two-thirds of the cost of the program. But you will still need premiums. You can make the 2 per cent deduction from the income on grain sales. This could be done when deliveries are made at the elevator, in just the same way as it was done in previous years under the prairie farm assistance program when there was a 1 per cent deduction. That method is simple, efficient and, most important, fair.
I submit that pay-outs should be made on an individual basis and not on a total area basis. I know that the minister and his officials want to come up with some system which will provide for pay-outs on a regional basis as opposed to a basis involving the whole Wheat Board area. That would be an improvement but it is still not good enough. Having a crop insurance and incomes plan will allow for individual pay-outs. Again, it remains contributory: the farmers will put up the money and pay into the plan individually and the deductions are made simply when they sell their grain. Actually, I suspect that a 2 per cent deduction from farmers would be sufficient to cover the premiums of both the income stabilization and the crop insurance programs. I did a little checking this morning and learned that less than 1 per cent of deductions based on grain sales in the province of Manitoba would have more than covered the premiums for crop insurance. If you raised the deduction to 2 per cent or 3 per cent, you would cover the premiums for all-risk crop insurance and income insurance.
A guaranteed price based on the cost of production has been an article of faith of my party for a long time. It was

in our election program of 1935, would you believe! We have raised this issue ever since, in every election. We have raised it in every parliament since then. Many countries of the world have done this. It is not socialistic. It is civilized; it is a proper way to deal with such an essential part of the economy of our nation. Moreover, it is the essential and proper way to deal equitably with grain farmers. In my opinion, that principle should apply to all agricultural production.
We are in favour of a system of guaranteed prices related to costs of production, and there should be variations in that to protect the farmer's net income. Since the end of the Second World War Canada has lost 400,000 families from farming; in other words, well over 1.25 million people have been driven from the land because of inadequate economic policies for agriculture. All parties can take some blame for this. Here we have a golden opportunity: we are legislating the beginning of an income program for grain farmers and it can lead the way and be an example to all other sectors of agriculture. Indeed, it can lead the way for all other parts of our economy. This could be a sensible and civilized incomes program.
Unfortunately, the bill is inadequate. Surely, in view of the attitude of the Government of Manitoba, which has criticized the contents of the legislation and pointed out most lucidly how the bill flies in the face of the principles of income stabilization, income guarantees or income insurance, unemployment insurance, hospital and medical insurance and principles to which private plans adhere, the government should listen. The members of the National Farmers Union have said the same thing. I have talked to members of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, and made it a point during the winter to talk to as many farmers as I could. These people are all perplexed and frustrated. They do not know what the legislation involves. They do not know what will happen. They do not know what the benefits will be if and when the bill passes.
As the bill now reads, some farmers could be adversely affected. Let me give an example. In my constituency a piece of railway track was washed out over a year ago and still has not been fixed. If the farmers of the area cannot deliver their grain and if their income drops as a consequence, they will not be covered under this legislation. They are not covered unless the whole grain industry suffers. You could also run into this situation: say that in one small corner of the western provinces, grain crops are of poor quality. We know that our customers want high grade, high protein grain. Assume that the rest of the Wheat Board area has grown high grade, high protein grain. Farmers in general have delivered lots of grain and farm incomes generally are high. But in this small corner where the grain is of low grade, low protein content, sales are poor and farm incomes drop. As the bill now reads, there will be no pay-out for them. The province of Manitoba makes the point that pay-outs should be on an individual basis; I submit that point is well taken.
Surely this is the sort of thing we should consider in committee. That is why, before this legislation passes, it should receive the scrutiny of the Standing Committee on Agriculture. The standing committee could spend all summer and fall talking to farmers; it is too late now, because the boys have just about finished spring seeding.
May 6, 1975

But the committee could start its work in late June and could continue holding meetings during the summer. The offices of farm organizations are open all summer. This might mean that a few members of parliament would have to work for a couple of weeks during the summer, but that is all right; we are already more than well paid and it would not hurt us a bit.
We could meet farmers and farm organizations all summer and return to this House in early September with a report and recommendations to the House on the basis of which the minister and his officials could draft a bill. We could get it through quickly and it could be the law of the land. We could establish a real grain income stabilization program which would be a crop insurance and income insurance program. It would be administered by the four western provinces, and the farmers would contribute to it. The government would contribute, but the provinces would pay the cost of operating the plan and each farmer would be eligible for benefit on an individual basis. The farmer's income would be protected.
Surely that is the least we can do. It is what we must do. Attempting to deal in committee, let alone in the House, with the legislation as drafted will result in nothing but frustration for farmers. As Manitoba says, it will be an exercise in frustration for all. So far as I am concerned, only the organizational genius of an ex-dean of law could implement a bill which reads as this one does. That reminds me of a story which happened in Britain. When the British parliament brought in rationing under Sir Winston Churchill's government during the Second World War, Nye Bevan got up and said something like this, "Mr. Speaker, England is an island full of coal, set in a sea full of fish, but only the organizational genius of the prime minister can see to it that we shall ration both."
Well, farmers in western Canada can grow grain like you wouldn't believe. Sometimes it is good quality, and sometimes it is not so good. Sometimes the crops are poor, and sometimes they are affected by events over which they have no control, whether is it weather or international developments or the Liberal government. But they have the ability to grow the stuff and they have the wherewithal, the machinery to ensure their incomes.
I can just see what the workers around London, Ontario, would say if you implemented an unemployment insurance program the same way as this grain stabilization program. You would have a riot on your hands. There is not a worker in the country who would stand for it. It is sheer nonsense for any government to be so dumb as to try to bring in legislation of this nature. I urge the government to study carefully what Manitoba is saying today before the committee on agriculture: they have five or six pages on what is wrong with the grain stabilization bill and what an income program should be, and they put it most succinctly and, I know, sincerely and positively. They are not looking for any fight with the federal government. They are, in a positive way, asking parliament and the government to reconsider its approach to a grains stabilization program.
The least we can do is take the subject matter of this bill to the farm organizations, the municipal organizations, the
Western Grain Stabilization
provincial governments and the crop insurance boards of all four western provinces, ask them how they would like it done and if they would like it done this way. If we did not get an almost unanimous negative response, I would be very surprised.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
In
speaking on this amendment, I made it very clear that all [The Acting Speaker (Mrs. Morin).]
parties in the House wish to provide for agriculture in all parts of Canada some form of insurance against instability of income. Yet, when we asked the government to let the principle of the bill be put before the farmers and let them decide whether they want it, the government refused that simple, democratic right to the farmers of western Canada.
When we proposed that one of the things that was concerning farmers in western Canada was that this was an agricultural matter, and agricultural matters should be the responsibility of the Minister of Agriculture and not of the Minister of Justice-the latter should look after matters such as abortion, which has nothing to do with grain income-the government refused to consider it. If we could only get the Minister of Justice off our backs a great deal of confidence could be engendered in the agricultural industry.

subsubtopic: PROCEEDS FROM THE PRODUCTION AND SALE OF WESTERN GRAIN
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: PROCEEDS FROM THE PRODUCTION AND SALE OF WESTERN GRAIN
speechtext:
On the
vital principle of voluntary or compulsory participation, the government refuses the farmers the right to decide what they want. Now we have to go into the committee with these principles established as the will of parliament; but I can assure you, Madam Speaker, that they are not the will of the farmer.
I did not speak in the early stages of the legislation for the simple reason that I wanted the House to hear the viewpoints of members of parliament who represent the farmers of western Canada, and most of them are on this side of the House. For 70 years, western Canada has borne the burden of Liberal parties on its back. For 70 years we have felt in the west that no one gave a damn for the interests of the western people. For years western farmers tended to be Liberal. Now you can see all across the country the reason why they are not any more, because when you ask for a chance for the farmers to express a view it is not given to them.
In spite of the minister in charge of the Wheat Board (Mr. Lang) and in spite of the whip the government applied to its members today, this bill is required in western Canada although not in the terms in which it is couched. This bill aims to do something that we have been talking about in the west for 35 years. I know that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) will agree with me when I say that one cannot solve the problems of agriculture piecemeal; they must be dealt with as a package. Just as we in the west know that we cannot attack the problem of the costs of agriculture, which are rising at 20 per cent a year, until we have resolved the problems of the people who live in the high-cost areas such as cities, so the city people in the east should recognize that they cannot solve their problems until we give a fair and equitable economic basis to all sections of the community-and that includes farmers. This bill should be part of a package; and the five points in that package are clear. The first point in building an agricultural policy should be the marketing of the produce of the farm to the people of the world who need food. The second principle should be stability of price. Over the last number of years, parliament has tried to deal with that problem through the Agricultural Stabilization Act which was put into place in 1959 and is being amended
May 6, 1975

Canada Elections Act

by the House now. It stabilizes prices to a degree and it is an insurance purely against disaster. It is a type of "stop loss" legislation, but it is fundamental as a base on which to build.
The third principle is stability of income. We have tried to deal with it under crop insurance. Crop insurance deals with the weather, and if you look at the statistics for western Canada today you will find that nearly two-thirds of all the farmers in the three prairie provinces have now educated themselves to the advantage of contributing to a fund that will protect them in times of crop loss. But that alone is not enough. The tremendous dips and dives of income over the last 70 years in western Canadian agriculture have made it the most risky of any industrial segment in Canada. It is this question of stabilizing incomes that this bill is all about. Before concluding the question of stability of incomes I should mention the other points in the package.
The fourth point is a modern system of farm credit. During the last 15 years, governments led by the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) and Liberal governments have tried their best to give us a modern system of farm credit, and in general it is doing very well.
