subsubtopic: PROVISION TO REVOKE PRIVILEGE OF VOTING BY PROXY IN FEDERAL ELECTIONS
speechtext:
that Bill C-232, to amend the Canada Elections Act (proxy voting), be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.
He said: Madam Speaker, a member of this House putting forward a private members' bill in the first instance wants to do two things: he would like to accomplish what his bill outlines, and if he is not successful in that he would like to direct the attention of the government toward the problem with which the bill deals. In this case the bill deals with the question of proxy voting. To me, the principle of one man, one vote is a sacred privilege which is part and parcel of most western democracies, and is a principle we should not tarnish in any way.
Many arguments have been made in the cause of proxy voting. Proxy votes are sought after and fought for in corporations and corporate empires. Some bitter feuds and fights take place over proxy votes in the corporate structure. It is not impossible to envisage proxy votes causing fights and squabbles within a constituency. It is a matter of who gets to the person who is unable to vote first, and in some instances who has him sign the paper. Then he is locked in, in the sense that his voting privileges are taken away while the facts or issues of the election may not have been explained to him. A voter may say, "It is nice of you to call. You knew I could not vote because I will not be in the country on voting day"-or it may be because of ill health-But it was nice of you to call and for that reason I will give you my vote." Three or four days later somebody may come along and reveal a different situation to the same voter, and the voter would have to say, "I am sorry, but I have given my proxy vote to your opposition." That situation could arise.
Much argument for proxy voting is sometimes centred around the thought that people who are hospitalized during an election cannot get to the polling station to vote. That is true in a federal election. It has never been

May 6, 1975
Canada Elections Act
explained to me why, in the province of Alberta, for example, ballot boxes in provincial elections have for years been taken to hospitals and hospitalized people have voted, but that in a federal election we are repeatedly told that that cannot happen, that the person has to appear at the polling station. In cases where they cannot, we now have the provision of proxy voting.
I think before the principle of one man, one vote is eroded in any way-this is merely a very small way but everything starts somewhere-all other avenues should be examined very closely. A case can be made in regard to invalids; they must have a doctor's certificate. A case can be made for a fisherman or prospector who is out of the country and therefore not able to vote.
It is interesting that from time to time we have 75 per cent or 78 per cent of the population taking part in a federal election. Sometimes the figure is closer to 70 per cent. In provincial elections it is lower than that, and in municipal elections lower still. It is interesting to note how many more people proxy voting has brought to polling stations and how many more fishermen and prospectors really wanted to take part, and took part, in the democratic procedure of voting. In the 1974 election, 6,915 people made use of the proxy voting privilege. That, to me, is a minuscule number. I would suggest that those who did use that privilege were badgered by political legmen from various political parties. If they had not been badgered, they might have showed up on voting day in any case.

subsubtopic: PROVISION TO REVOKE PRIVILEGE OF VOTING BY PROXY IN FEDERAL ELECTIONS
speechtext: The Conservatives are guilty of that.

subsubtopic: PROVISION TO REVOKE PRIVILEGE OF VOTING BY PROXY IN FEDERAL ELECTIONS
speechtext:
Conservatives are guilty of that, yes, but I would like to think they are no more guilty than Liberals.
I do not appreciate the erosion of the principle of one man, one vote. The other system works fine in a corporate structure where big business deals with money; money buys power, power buys votes, and so forth. That kind of thing has gone on for years within the corporate structure, but I do no think it enhances our democracy to see it within out voting system.
Proxy voting will remain if my bill tonight is defeated, but if it is sent to committee I would suggest that the committee consider its application. With proxy voting today, the returning officer has to witness the signature of the person who wants to give up his right to vote. That may work well in a city riding where there is a high population density, such as in downtown Toronto, Montreal, Calgary or Edmonton. I can say that it does not work very well in a widely scattered riding where the returning officer may live in one corner of the riding.

speakerposition: Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: PROVISION TO REVOKE PRIVILEGE OF VOTING BY PROXY IN FEDERAL ELECTIONS
speechtext: He has to drive miles and miles.

subsubtopic: PROVISION TO REVOKE PRIVILEGE OF VOTING BY PROXY IN FEDERAL ELECTIONS
speechtext:
That is quite right; the returning officer had to drive miles and miles to an invalid, to people who are not going to be in the constituency, to people who are leaving on holidays or for prospecting, and to students who are out of the constituency. Students out of the constituency now have the right to vote at the university they are attending. There should be greater safeguards if proxy voting is to continue. The committee should propose greater safeguards against abuses which may arise. That will certainly make the application of proxy voting apply

more fairly throughout the various parts of one's constituency and throughout Canada.
I believe that proxy voting opens the door to widespread abuses which will only grow as people become familiar with the concept. It is interesting that in the 1972 election there were 1,309 people in rural areas who used proxy voting. In urban areas-basically, city and suburbia-8,389 people used proxy voting. I think that clearly demonstrates that it is a privilege given to those living in proximity to the returning officer and not to those living miles away.
It is of value to our democratic system that steps should be taken to allow hospitalized people to exercise their federal vote as they do their provincial vote. We should not weaken the importance of the duty of the citizens of Canada. We should not minimize that duty by allowing them to barter their vote to someone who may suggest that their interest will be looked after; that if they sign a piece of paper the right man will be elected.
This bill is a small thing, but so are most initial steps. We must face the fact that the abuses of proxy voting will increase. I choose this way to register my opposition to anything which lessens the duty that each man assumes when he accepts citizenship. We see lobbying for votes going on within the power structures of corporations. Sometimes such votes are bought and sold, and there is nothing to stop this happening in our democracy. While we might say it will never happen, that such things do not happen in elections, we all know that elections cost money. A voter wants to know what promises the politicians will give in the way of legislation or better treatment for people.
We have just witnessed the evils uncovered by Watergate in the United States and I think it is safe to say that most Canadians were upset. I am not suggesting that proxy voting at some future election would cause a similar situation in Canada, but it could be the beginning of something nearly as bad. I know, Madam Speaker, that my conscience will rest a little better from having put this bill forward at this time. I hope the House will send the bill to committee so that the whole question of proxy voting can be examined by the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.

subsubtopic: PROVISION TO REVOKE PRIVILEGE OF VOTING BY PROXY IN FEDERAL ELECTIONS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I do not think the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) and I disagree on the substantive issue of proxy voting, although there might be some disagreement on the procedural aspect of the question. The history of democracy is tied to the right to vote, but the right to vote should not be moulded to fit a system. Rather, the system should be flexible enough to permit that all qualified people, all citizens, will have the opportunity to vote. The hon. member for Crowfoot said that voting is a privilege. I might add that it is also a right and duty. It is not a right that was arrived at by simply talking about freedom. He also said that due to the abuses of proxy voting, people might be badgered, I think was his word. It is my understanding that in a democracy such as we have in Canada, we subscribe to the idea of advise and consent.
May 6, 1975

The hon. member pointed out that only 6,900 people voted by proxy in the last general election. That is a minuscule number compared to the total number of voters, but it was an important opportunity for those 6,900 people who exercised their right to vote. This is about the same number as voted by proxy in 1972, but we should remember that in 1972 many more students used the proxy vote because school was out at the time of the vote.
In a press release of September 12, 1972, Jean-Marc Hamel, the Chief Electoral Officer, estimated that at least
10,000	eligible citizens studying overseas would be left out of the voting procedure: a great number of people living or working overseas before the date of the first advance poll would be left out as well. The only people outside Canada who could vote in the election were civil servants, members of the armed forces and dependants of both categories. These numbered approximately 110,000. Their ballots were taken prior to election day so that they could reach Canada in time to be counted with the regular election returns.
The problem for students arises in determining the place of ordinary residence, particularly in the case of the single student living away from home but who still has his residence in the home of his parents or guardian. In the instructions to student voters away from home, four categories are defined. Married or single students living at home offer no problem; they simply vote at the polling division in which their home is located. In the case of married students, this would be the residence where they were physically residing on enumeration day.
The single student on his own, in other words financially independent of his parents, can vote where he is physically residing on enumeration day. The single student living away from home but dependent on his parents or guardian is the only one eligible to vote by proxy. This is a multistep procedure involving a variety of forms and is outlined in the Canada Elections Act.
Many people who were interested in having a voice as to who would govern the country were disappointed at the timing of the last election. I do not place the blame on either side of the House for that, but accept it as a fait accompli. These people felt cheated, however, because they were not able to vote and because as the law stands they were not treated as equals.
I suggest that proxy voting is not the only way we can get around our problems, but it is the one way we have devised to solve the problem of those who want to take advantage of their rights as citizens of Canada to have a voice in their government. I put forward another suggestion: perhaps we should consider establishing a permanent voters' list. It does not seem fair that we should do all this in such a rush. The hon. member mentioned that there were abuses.
Of course, errors may be made but they are errors of omission and commission. Efforts must be made to ensure that all Canadians have a chance to vote for the men and women who will represent them in this House.
Canada Elections Act

I urge, as does the hon. member for Crowfoot, that more consideration should be given to this question. Let us assure all our citizens that they have a voice; that they have a chance to mould the future or our beloved Canada.

subsubtopic: PROVISION TO REVOKE PRIVILEGE OF VOTING BY PROXY IN FEDERAL ELECTIONS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, there are occasions when my hon. friend from Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) comes into this House with good ideas. There are days when he makes an awfully good case, whether the idea is good or not. I do not think this is one of those days. Actually, so far as this bill is concerned it does not matter whether it is rejected or talked out. I do not think it should get any more consideration than it will be given during the present private members' hour.
The hon. member for Crowfoot talked about abuses. No doubt there are abuses under the Canada Elections Act and there are abuses in election campaigns; but I submit that the percentage of abuses involving proxy voting is perhaps the lowest there is in the whole election machinery. The hon. member gave the statistic I wanted, that in the last election 6,915 persons exercised the proxy voting privilege. If you divide that figure by 264, it comes out to an average of 26 per constituency. That makes sense to me, because in my constituency, Winnipeg North Centre, the number was about 18.
I can go further and say I checked the list at the office of the returning officer in my constituency. I found that I knew, or knew of, just about every name on the list; I knew those who were for me and those who were against me. Most, of course, were for me. It was clear to me that every one of them was a person who was in hospital or in a nursing home, or confined to his own home and, hence, not able to cast his vote except under the provisions of the proxy voting regulations. The 18 votes in Winnipeg North Centre did not make any difference to the outcome of the election in that constituency, and I suggest that the 6,915 votes across Canada did not make any difference to the make-up of this parliament. But, as the hon. member who just spoke so well put it, their privilege to vote made a great deal of difference to those particular persons. They were given a right to participate in a general election, a right which previous to 1972 such persons did not have.
Actually, I think this is one of the most humane improvements we made to the Canada Elections Act the last time we revised it. We did not make a sweeping change that could result in a different outcome at an election, but we respected the right of the ill, the handicapped and the shut in to exercise their franchise at election time. It was the humane and decent thing to do, and I hope that under no circumstance will this House consider revoking that right. That, of course, is what would happen if the bill before us were passed.
Some changes still need to be made. Perhaps the proxy voting system needs to be enlarged. I found that a half dozen or more people who wanted the right to exercise a proxy vote under the regulations were not able to do so because the regulations are just a little too strict. I remember, when we were enacting this legislation, that we accepted the proposition that we had to tie it up so tightly that there would not be abuse. Perhaps what we should

May 6, 1975
Canada Elections Act
look at is not a proposal to cancel this right but a proposal to extend it.
In the same way, we must consider the whole question of advance polls. In this area we run into many frustrating experiences. The advance polls are further ahead now than they used to be, and they do accommodate quite a number of people, but in every election there are individuals who will be away and who will not be able to vote either on the general polling day or at the advance polls.
We must also consider the question of absentee voting, which now takes place in a number of provinces but still does not apply in a federal election. My hon. friend from Crowfoot says we must guard against abuse and make sure we do not erode the integrity of our electoral system. But, on the other side of the coin, we must make sure that every Canadian citizen who has the legal right to vote has that right in a practical sense. Therefore, I hope the House will not support this bill. I have no objection to the hon. member's introducing it, in the sense that by doing so he has raised election issues. It gives us a chance to air some of these things, and I express the hope, already expressed across the way, that we will take another look at advance polls, absentee voting, and so on.
When we talk about proxy voting, I think mainly of those who are ill. I think particularly of a quite well known woman in Winnipeg, a victim of multiple-sclerosis who spent a long time in hospital and who worked for this right to vote for many years. I think of how much it meant to her when, after years of not being able to vote, she was able to do so. I think that a large percentage of the 6,915 people who voted by means of proxy in the last election were Canadian citizens who suffered from illness of one kind or another, and they feel just a little better as Canadian citizens because they had the right to vote.
I emphasize that under the proxy regulations there are serious restrictions: the proxy has to be obtained in advance of election day; there must be a visit to the office of the returning officer; there must be various signatures, and so on. The person who will do the proxy voting has to be on the list in the same polling division as the person for whom the proxy vote is to be cast; he must be acceptable to the person for whom he will vote, and no one may cast a proxy vote for more than one person. I suggest that the protections in the regulations are pretty good; that we should not restrict this right but, rather, that we should look at the other side of the picture and make sure we are providing all possible ways for Canadian citizens who have the legal right to vote to exercise that right, in fact, on election day.
I have been rather strong in my criticisms of the bill proposed by the hon. member for Crowfoot. Perhaps he likes it that way. I am glad he raised the issue and gave us the chance to have this discussion, but hope this bill will not pass. I want the proxy vote to remain.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to make a few remarks on Bill C-232 introduced by the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner). First I want to congratulate him for the courage he has demonstrated in introducing this bill. At first sight, I had felt that proxy

voting would provide a few more people with the right to vote. This legislation is very difficult to administer. In my own riding, a number of people tried during the last election to avail themselves of this proxy voting. It is quite an involved process, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) indicated a while ago: obtain the necessary papers from the returning officer, meet the person who will not come to vote and obtain a proxy to cast a vote on his or her behalf. There are people who will cover 100 or 125 miles to fetch a little piece of paper. During the last election, in my own riding, a farmer with the best intentions wanted his son, a university student, to vote. He took the necessary steps, spent three or four days getting all these papers together, and when voting day came, he went to the poll to cast a vote on behalf of his son, just to be told that a student had already been there to cast a vote on behalf of his son. It happens sometimes that overly zealous people go and vote on behalf of others. With such a system as the one we have now, a person can very easily vote for about 10 others the very same day.
Such irregularities will occur so long as we do not have the identity card called for. I could give evidence to support my case. The big parties have it very easy today. They have a majority and are well organized. As for us, the cost of contacting in our ridings for instance a hundred or so people who would vote by proxy and ensuring that it is done in an orderly way would be prohibitive. A special collection would have to be made to pay the costs of getting in touch with those people. In my riding, three persons voted by proxy. And when I was asked for explanations I said: Don't make useless applications, it is too much trouble, costs too much and leads to nothing.
So, we might as well cross out the amendment, but anyway it is before the House and I am sure the government will want to let things stand, but there are other ways. I heard someone say earlier: It seeks to allow all people, as many people as possible, to vote. I would agree if that enabled everybody to vote, but vote themselves, and not have somebody else vote for them. There is a difference, because no one knows whom the person who will do the proxy voting will vote for.
With respect to proxy voting, we are told that people who have to stay in hospital cannot go to the polling station. I wish to draw the attention of the Chair, because it is a point which will require an amendment from the government. To end the ridiculous situation in hospitals, we should take up the method used in the provinces, establish one, two or three polling stations, and go from one room to the next, as in Quebec, to have everyone vote themselves instead of voting by proxy.
At the last election, we were told there would be a polling station in the hospital, and suddenly the organizers of a large party decided that, since there were too many Social Crediters in there, there would be no polling station in the hospital. We lost 510 voters, because 80 per cent of those people in the hospital voted for me. So they just closed the polling station there. This is merely an indication-
I did not care, Madam Speaker, I had enough people voting for me, but those people were not given the opportunity to exercize their rights as citizens as freely as

anyone else, and that is the point I am making, that it is not fair. They should, yes-

speechtext:
That goes on to a larger extent in big cities. I have already seen what happened in cities. The same kind of thing went on on a larger scale in hospitals. They say it is not possible to have everybody vote by going around bedrooms. In large hospitals, if one voting station is not enough, they set up two, three or four. But in my constituency, they even established voting stations at the last minute for 50 voters in the forest. A poll was opened and delegates had to be sent 125 miles away to lumberjacks who had already voted on Saturday in their parishes, before leaving. They had already voted in their parishes. A poll was opened for them. That is why I say it is very easy, because we must not forget that all lumberjacks come down from the forest on Friday nights. They know very well that there are temporary polls. No need to fear, the temporary polls close. They have a poll in the forest. This often doubles the number of voters. I would be in favour of establishing many polls in hospitals so that all sick people may be visited and vote in their rooms.
All the provinces do it: why couldn't the federal government? Why? At the provincial level, it is considered fair; it would only be fair and equitable for all the sick to be able to vote in their rooms. To my mind that is the main point. Even if this bill was introduced merely to discuss this point, I invite the government to study it, because the problem exists right across Canada.
I had an unfortunate experience in my riding, but for the sick people, every election is an unfortunate experience. Of course, after the election, it is maddening to have 500 fewer votes than were expected! But what revolts me is that the democratic system is not respected by small time politicians who exist to foul everything, to keep those who do not share their ideas from voicing theirs. As for me, I respect every party in my riding, whether blue, white or red, and that is why almost everyone votes for me because I respect and defend them. I went to these hospitals, and was asked to bring this to the government's attention, in order that this same error does not happen next time. Because errors of this kind happened a number of times. And then there is the identity card error.
We have been proposing the identity card for more than ten years. This would be fair to the voter. After all, everyone has his social security number in his pocket. Why not add a photograph, this would double up as an identity card. The voter coming to the poll with his identity card cannot be mistaken for somebody else. But of course this would not suit the old parties.
With everything that is being done at election time, democracy is going down the drain. Quite often families living next to a poll do not vote, through laziness or otherwise. I believe the Canada Elections Act should be more stringent. Voting should be compulsory. If a citizen is too lazy to do his duty, he should be forced to. I also found it has come to the point where you have to pick up people at their homes so they will vote. Sometimes people living next door to the poll. If you do not pick them up, they will not vote. Can you imagine that? And then they
Canada Elections Act
say they have done their citizen's duty. I welcome this bill because it gives us an opportunity to point out to the government weaknesses in our electoral legislation. We are all elected members, and we are all interested in bringing justice to the people. Even if the bill is not discussed in committee, I expect the government will bring some amendments to the Canada Elections Act, which is often somewhat undemocratic.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have always had the belief out west that the eastern barons were after us, and I am very surprised to hear that the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) is going to be put in the class of these eastern barons, because obviously he is trying to take something away from the west. Perhaps I should not just say the west because the same thing could be said of the east coast. If the hon. member has not heard, we have a fair fishing industry along the west coast of British Columbia, and I understand the same can be said of the maritimes.
I think the hon. member for Crowfoot would have to agree that one thing the government should not be doing is trying to discourage people from voting. We have enough problems getting people to realize that the government they elect will control their lives and that they cannot be apathetic about voting. If the hon. member for Crowfoot had mulled this bill over a bit he would have realized that it is not the role of a government or politician to discourage people from voting.
I am glad to see the hon. member has come back into the chamber, because I want to tell him that in the northern part of my riding we have no roads or railroads. But we do have people who are prospectors, and although they do not have television sets or radios in many instances, they do have proxy voting. And here is the hon. member for Crowfoot trying to take away one of the few small things in life that these people up there have. At least at election time they have their proxy and they can vote. It may not be much, but they do have a proxy vote.
Perhaps I am being a little facetious in saying this, but one of the experiences I had when I ran for the first time in the last federal election was going to hospitals where there were people who were either sick or infirm because of age, and I was surprised at the amount of interest shown by them and at what it meant to them to be able to vote. I am sure many members must have had the same experience. It certainly brought something into their lives. This may sound a very small point, but when people are infirm, especially the elderly, an election gives them something to talk about among themselves, something to which they can look forward.

I think the hon. member is sincere in his question. First, I do not know the exact number in my riding who used the proxy vote. I do know that in 1974 in British Columbia 650 people used the proxy vote. Interest-

ingly enough, in 1972 the number was 601, so the two figures were very close.
My point, which I think was emphasized before, is that I do not care if there is only one person who took advantage of the proxy vote in British Columbia-I would retain it in British Columbia for that one person, to make sure that all those who wished to vote have the opportunity to vote. I do not think the hon. member realizes that many fishermen do not go out to fish just for a day or two but for several weeks at a time. These are the sort of people we should be considering, just as we should consider prospectors. I do not think people fully realize that all Canadians do not live in cities, that all Canadians do not have the same facilities.
If I were asked for suggestions to improve the situation, I would extend proxy voting to the sort of person who works in the woods, who lives in Vancouver but works on northern Vancouver Island. These people should be given proxy voting because they are away from home for several weeks at a time, and they do not return home from a distance of 400 or 500 miles just to vote. As I said earlier, it is the responsibility of the government to encourage people to vote, not to discourage them.
I suppose I will be accused of speaking against this bill, and I apologize-I should not have used the term "baron from Alberta". However, sometimes we regard them as easterners too.
I was interested to note that Ontario and Nova Scotia headed the list in federal proxy voting. My theory is that we have not done a good enough job telling people about the proxy vote. I do not think people do not wish to use the proxy. Our information service has not been of the highest calibre. This is a relatively new act, and the 1972 election was the first one in which it took effect. As time passes I hope that more and more people will realize this right does exist and will utilize it. It is up to rite and to the hon. member for Crowfoot to do the job of making sure people are aware of this.
I would seriously oppose the suggestion that this privilege of voting by proxy be taken from people who, because of their occupation, are unable to attend the advance polls or the polls on election day. Perhaps we do not have the facilities in my area that the hon. member for Crowfoot has, although his is a rural riding also. The northern part of Vancouver Island lacks roads and certainly railroads, and in many cases boats are the only form of travel.
The provision for the proxy vote was well designed to meet a certain need. In the area of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) I would assume that the proxy vote is used by people who are in hospitals. This is a humanitarian provision adopted by the government and members of parliament. It has been extended to those people who would not be able to vote normally. Surely hon. members agree with the principle. There may be different ways of carrying this out, but surely we all agree that the proxy vote has been a good provision. I suggest that anything we can do as members of parliament to encourage the Canadian public to vote is a step in the right direction, and I say that very sincerely.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I should like to say a few words on this matter in the short time we have available. I believe this has been a worthwhile and constructive discussion if nothing else, and for that reason, and because he had the courage to bring this matter forward, the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) deserves congratulations. This is the type of thing that should be discussed at times in the House.
Mention has been made by the hon. member for St. Catharines (Mr. Parent) of a permanent voters' list. Perhaps this is something that should be considered along with the suggestion of placing ballot boxes in hospitals, nursing homes, and elsewhere. There should be a better method for mariners, prospectors and fishermen to exercise their right to vote. These and other matters have been considered today. Does the government really intend to consider ideas and suggestions of this nature? These are things that should be given some priority of attention within the duration of this parliament.
There is one thing that does bother me in respect of the proxy vote provision contained in the Canada Elections Act. Citizens have the right to vote, and it is a right. We should make it convenient for all citizens to exercise that right. The thing that bothers me is that this provision does not enhance the right to vote, it provides an individual with the right to transfer that vote to somebody else. The right to vote should be a personal thing. The vote is a right one must exercise by one's self. I believe the intention of the government and parliament when this measure was enacted was to give those persons listed in Section 46 the opportunity to vote. I wonder if the provision does not in fact give them the opportunity to transfer that right.
There are several sections of the Canada Elections Act that should be deleted or amended, and I should like to take this opportunity to refer to them in the House. One involves the requirement that the leader of a so-called recognized party, or his delegate, must provide a certificate to be filed with the nomination papers of a candidate. To my mind this is very undemocratic, and this act should be democratic, just like the right to vote and the right to be a candidate. These should be rights just as is the right to exercise the franchise in as convenient a manner as possible, without coming under a fascist rule.
I trust this discussion will be considered by the government and that something will come of the comments that have been made here today on some very worthwhile and necessary matters.

Madam Speaker, I am overwhelmed. I should like to say in the few minutes left to us that we have had some discussions to determine what can be done to provide an opportunity for members of parliament to take a close look at the Canada Elections Act. It has been the practice in past parliaments that after an election has taken place there should be an opportunity for members to have a close look at amendments to the act and to promote ideas they have to change it, bringing it more in line with changes that have taken place in Canadian society.
I might say that the idea for a proxy vote arose from the discussions that took place in the privileges and elections
Western Grain Stabilization
committee following the 1968 election. Anyone who looks at the regulations governing the proxy vote will find that not only is the act drawn very finely, but the regulations which permit those people qualified under the act to participate in proxy voting are also drawn very narrowly. We have experimented through two elections with the proxy vote, and I think most members would say this has worked out reasonably well and the abuses we feared have not developed.
There are other groups in society who should be provided for under the act. We should be looking at other areas in order to extend the opportunity to vote in Canadian elections to as many eligible people as possible. While the proxy voting procedure may not be the most ideal, perhaps there are other ways in addition to the suggestion of the hon. member for Moncton (Mr. Jones) of allowing people to cast their votes without having to go through the necessity of delegating the right. In the period of time we have from the opening of advance polls it may be possible that the returning officer in a given community could go around to those places or residences of those people who are unable to get out to vote. subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING THE STABILIZATION OF NET PROCEEDS FROM THE PRODUCTION AND SALE OF WESTERN GRAIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the House rose at five o'clock I was outlining the five basic points or fundamentals that go to the establishment of a logical and coherent policy on agriculture. First and most important is marketing. Second is stability of price. Third is stability of income, and fourth is a modern farm credit system.

Western Grain Stabilization
The fifth fundamental is the redevelopment of the industry to meet the new challenges and needs of an ever changing world.
In order to provide this package everything must be coordinated. Our policy must be based on one sound principle leading to the next one. This bill, C-41, should be a part of this package. It should enable the farmer to insure himself against the vagaries of income. As I mentioned earlier, the crop insurance legislation is doing a fairly good job in allowing the farmer to have some money to insure himself against the vagaries of weather, but on top of that we should build an insurance program so that he may be ensured a fair rate of income. For some reason or other the government has chosen not to keep this program within this package of a logical, coherent policy leading to the objective of a stable, healthy, agricultural industry designed to meet the demands of the world.
We have this particular bill introduced in effect under the Canadian Wheat Board Act. The Canadian Wheat Board Act has nothing to do with stability of income in respect of agriculture. The C.W.B. is purely a marketing device to set prices. So, on the first test this legislation is not part of a coherent and logical package to help agriculture. Also, it should be under the Minister of Agriculture.
The second point about this bill is that legislation dealing with agriculture should treat all farmers alike. We have farmers in eastern Canada, and with them we associate the farmers of British Columbia, who are quite different in respect of their techniques and the products they grow from the grain farmers on the prairies. One reason is geography. Essentially we have a desert area which man has learned to master and has made into a great food source for the world. The other parts of Canada have different types of agriculture based on different soils, moisture, different heat units, and so on.
Here we are bringing in legislation by which the parliament of Canada gives one sort of a deal to the farmers of one part of Canada, and yet in no place in the government's legislation is there an opportunity to offer the same deal to all the farmers. So, on the essential question of the unity of the Canadian people in this industry of agriculture we have again divided the east and the west. This seems to be part and parcel of the attitude of the Liberal party when it is in power.
Second, on this question of treating farmers alike, there is a tremendous clash today in western Canada, for example, between the pure grain farmers and the livestock farmers. What is good for one industry sometimes hurts another industry. We are going through one of those periods now. With the present technology, livestock such as poultry, hogs, and cattle now require tremendous volumes of grain. The sudden rise in the price of feed grain in the world markets two years ago has wreaked havoc not only in Canada but all over the world with the price of red meat and the cost of producing it. Here in this bill we have in effect added and exaggerated the difference between the wants and needs of the livestock industry and the grain industry.
The third point, which bears on the first point, is that farmers look above all to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. 
Whelan) to be their spokesman in parliament on all matters concerning their welfare. They have seen the Department of Agriculture over the last ten years split and divided among four ministers.
Agriculture now comes under the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce through the structure of the Grains Council. Agriculture also comes under the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang). What abortion has to do with agriculture, we are never quite certain, but they are put together by this government. Agriculture also comes under the Minister of Agriculture once in a while; it comes under the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson) and, if you want to take all the other things with which it is associated, it also comes under the Department of Finance. But my main point is that we have seen the breaking down of the agricultural industry into little parts in so far as the administration of the affairs of agriculture in the last ten years are concerned.
I put this down to the fact that we have begun to worship here in Ottawa the idea that everything should be turned away from parliament, from the control of ministers, and put into the hands of technocrats who look at it from the point of view of diagrams on the wall. When a new department is set up, they put a certain number of squares on the minister's chart which, I suppose, give him prestige equal to that of other ministers. They look for some department from which to rob activities, and so the ARDA program came out of the Department of Agriculture and agricultural rehabilitation was put under another minister. No matter how well intentioned that other minister may be toward agriculture, the people in his department are not in contact with agriculture, their main interest being something else.
Likewise with the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act-it was taken out of the Department of Agriculture. Here we have a whole section that was once the pride and joy of the Minister of Agriculture because prairie farm rehabilitation had brought a huge area, almost 1,000 miles in width, back into productivity after the great drought. It was an example all over the world of what could be done when technology and science were applied to a difficult program in so far as geography, soil and climate conditions are concerned.
This once proud division of the Department of Agriculture lies dormant. The division, which used to number 120 engineers ten years ago, is now reduced to 80, and as the years go by and some will retire there will be less of them. Nothing is given them to do. I have seen what a group of men can accomplish in bringing an area back into productivity. I know how much has to be done, and my only comment about PFRA is not that the objectives have been changed but that that program has been taken out of the Department of Agriculture and put under another department which has nothing to do with agriculture.
The men sit there waiting for their pensions. Yet we have so much to do, not only in rehabilitating the soil on the prairies-which should be done not only on the prairies but all across the country-but also in bringing this program back under the Department of Agriculture and applying it in the Atlantic area, the northern parts of Quebec and Ontario, and even the settled parts of these provinces, as well as in the valleys in British Columbia.
May 6, 1975

The great experience and technical know how of these men in rehabilitating soil and making it productive should be put to use. Once again I point out that there should be one minister in charge of the bulk of the agricultural divisions.
The minister who has particularly concerned us in western Canada has been the Minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board. He is obviously able. He passed all his exams in school, became the dean of law at the university of Saskatchewan, and came down here to become Minister of Justice-a tribute to his ability and seriousness. But it was a calamity to us in the west to have this inflexible man put in charge of our most vital possession, the ability to produce high protein wheat in dry land farming. He is not content to look after the Department of Justice and the Canadian Wheat Board. We hear announcements in the west that he deals with transportation there, and with labour problems, in fact with anything that concerns the west. No other minister is allowed to interfere in these matters.
We hardly see the Minister of Agriculture in the West. All the announcements about justice, transportation, regional economic expansion and everything else seem to come from the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang). Everything this minister has touched, as many hon. members have made very clear, has turned out to be bad for us. I cannot name all the things, let me say simply that the LIFT program is on the lips of every western farmer. They were sold down the river on the basis of false statistics, they were taken out of production, and when the demand came and the price went up from $2 to $5 a bushel, many farmers did not have too much grain to sell, not to mention the fact that hungry people could have done with the extra 300 million bushels that would have been produced.
Then there is the grain exchange. For two or three generations farmers fought to get grain under the Canadian Wheat Board, and this minister said he was considering it for the handling of feed grain, but only considering it. Throughout the election that was fought last summer he said that was not the policy of the government, just a series of things which, as a good minister, he was considering. But, the minute the election was over, feed grains were put under the grain exchange.
Then there is the question of inland terminals. It goes back to 1921 when this was first proposed. There is the choice between a system ensuring the lowest cost of handling grain in the inland system or establishing a grain system that would be in harmony with the social and economic needs of the west. The inland terminal is economically sound for those who own it, but disastrous for the people who live within its shadow.
Next we come to the Crowsnest pass rates. This country, out of its desire to have a national railway, gave large chunks of land, great tracts of forest, and great areas of mineral wealth to the CPR in return for a guarantee that the grain from the prairies would be moved into position at a fixed rate.
Everyone knows that with the technology of the last 80 years the cost of moving bulk products has decreased year by year. Yet we see a program beginning, which seems to happen every time there is a lapse of about 10 years, to persuade the people of Canada that the Crowsnest pass
Western Grain Stabilization
rate deal must be broken. Who was it brought this to public attention? Naturally the men who run the railways would love to get at this helpless captive prisoner, the wheat farmer. They would just love to get their rates and charge the farmer the same price American farmers are charged to haul their grain to markets. American farmers did not give away half a continent to a group of men to build their railway.
I simply ask who brought this Crowsnest pass rate back into public discussion again? Sitting in this House 10 years ago the minister in charge of transport said that the Crowsnest pass rate would never be raised again. He became the head of the Canadian Transportation Commission eventually. I am referring to Mr. Pickersgill.
Who brings this back in? Who roused all the western farmers this last eight or nine months? It was the Minister of Justice. Then, when all the fires are burning, and every farmer and every group is talking about it, he says that it was just a personal opinion. A legislative chamber in Saskatchewan voted a resolution opposing it. The Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau) had to send a wire repudiating his minister, by saying that it was just personal views he was expressing.
Why does the minister keep stirring everything up? Everything he stirs up is to get westerners alarmed about the possibility that the government is going back to its traditional practice of goosing the west.
Railway line abandonment is coming up this year. We were promised in this House 10 years ago that no railway line would be abandoned until we obtained all the information about traffic on each line and until each line produced the operating costs. It was not until this year that a bill was introduced into this House forcing the railways to give us this information.
Who should be our defender in these matters? It should be the Minister of Agriculture, but he is left wandering around in Ontario. We have no one speaking for agriculture in the west.
We had a little trouble on the west coast last year. Negotiations were going on under the principle of collective bargaining. Two ministers of the Crown went out and interfered with that collective bargaining procedure. It was not that we lost so much money on the wages we paid the terminal workers, but during the period of the strike we lost $12 million in demurrage, and the government refuses to pay for its own mistakes. Those two babes in blunderland wandering around out there cost us heavily.
Last year we had a debate across the country on resource taxation. The Minister of Justice even moves into finance and lays down an ultimatum in western Canada that those provinces are not going to push the federal government around, at a time when the provinces were fighting to get and hold control of what was theirs.
I would say that this is more than just a bill to stabilize net income. It is a tragedy that it has to be fought on this wider issue. This afternoon we gave the minister and the government a chance to withdraw from their position and let the farmers decide, after they have heard discussions of the bill, what principles they want. There was no flexibili-

May 6, 1975
Western Grain Stabilization
ty or willingness to give the farmers a chance. We are seeing the same technique as we saw on the LIFT program. What the government decides is the law of the Medes and Persians. This is infallibility speaking, this is the ex cathedra announcement, and the farmer is not allowed to express his viewpoint. He will express it all right, after we have committed ourselves to principles which may not be acceptable to him.
It is clear that all parties, as well as the government, want to do something about the stabilization of the income of grain farmers. Hopefully the government wants to do the same thing for all farmers, but there are certain things which have to be done before any form of sound approach can be taken.
What is missing in this basic foundation? If we are to stabilize income and if we are to stabilize price, we should first ensure that it is possible for farmers to produce the maximum amount. Second, we should ensure that it is possible to sell all that is grown or produced. The first step in giving the farmer real security of income in the production of grain is to give him markets at a fair price. There used to be long term agreements with eight or nine different countries. Where are they now? We still have the agreement with China, but that is all.
From 1945 to 1967 the grain farmers of the world had an international commodity agreement. They set a floor and a ceiling price for three year periods. Where is that agreement now? It is gone because this government connived with the American government to get rid of the international wheat agreement. This government had a new philosophy: sell at any price; that it called competition. The government sent farm income plunging down in the years 1969, 1970 and 1971, after it destroyed the international wheat agreement.
In February, 1972, led by the Saskatchewan wheat pool, the farmers of this country joined with the farmers of the United States, Australia and Argentina, went to see the United States Secretary of Agriculture in Washington and pleaded with him to let the price of grain go to its real price because there was a shortage of grain. On this minister's orders, we kept selling grain during the winter of 1972 at a price below the cost of production. Then we ran out of grain, and I, along with the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. Hamilton), made the statement that we were running out of grain.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING THE STABILIZATION OF NET PROCEEDS FROM THE PRODUCTION AND SALE OF WESTERN GRAIN
speechtext:
The
minister has always acted on behalf of the system, and if the system has statistics which say there is a surplus, he says there is a surplus. These figures were wrong 20 years ago, they were wrong 10 years ago, and they are wrong today. And that is not the end of it. If we examine the same source of information with regard to beef in North America and Canada we find that in the last five years, according to the statistics this government takes as gospel truth because they come from a computer using a formula, we in Canada consumed 7 per cent more beef than we produced and imported.
The same applies in the United States. They are supposed to have been consuming over the last five years 9 per cent more beef than they produced and imported. So we have this silly situation of farmers being told by governments that the people concerned have produced more beef than they did this last ten years because the figures said so. How asinine! Those figures are just as wrong for beef as they are for wheat. The minister has not learned anything. He is like the Bourbons-he forgets nothing and learns nothing.
We need an international wheat agreement. Instead of talking about getting rid of the Crowsnest Pass rates the government should take the lead, as the government did in 1932, and also after the Second World War in 1946 and 1949, and get an international wheat agreement. Roughly 80 per cent of bread grain going into export markets today comes from the United States and Canada. Our two countries together could make an agreement. We could tie up with Argentina and Australia which would always follow good leadership. But we have a Prime Minister lying in the sun down in the Caribbean saying, "I am not going to join a cartel that sets prices for producers. I do not care about any sort of producer in Canada." This minister is just regurgitating what the Prime Minister is thinking.
Without a basic world price level and floor, Mr. Speaker, there will be no income stability, regardless of how many laws we pass and how much money we put into a fund.
If an incomes policy is to be put on top of a good international floor price there should be a good domestic foundation on which to build. Such a foundation is in place, and the Conservative Party is willing to tell the government how to administer the program if the minister does not know. There is already a workable crop insurance plan in place for which all the figures have been worked out. The federal-provincial machinery is working smooth-
May 6, 1975

ly, and the farmers like and trust the program. All that has to be done is build this income stabilization plan on top of the crop insurance program on an individual basis.
This afternoon the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) read into the record portions of a brief prepared for submission to the Senate Committee on Agriculture by the Manitoba Crop Insurance Corporation and the Manitoba Department of Agriculture. I should like to quote from the same brief, beginning with the last paragraph on page 8, as follows:
We regret to say, Mr. Chairman, that if that were the objective of the proposed Prairie Grain Stabilization Act, it could not be achieved by the measures envisaged in Bill C-41.
They are referring to protection of income here. It continues:
What is more serious in our view, however, is the fact that Bill C-41 does not have as its specific purpose the protection of farmers against losses due to economic events beyond their control. One of the most exasperating aspects of the bill is that it is next to impossible to detect the rationale behind it, and this lack of rationale together with the extreme complexity of the bill make any attempt at explaining this important legislation to farmers an exercise in frustration.
This is the view of the Crop Insurance Corporation of Manitoba. It will be the same in Saskatchewan and Alberta. Yesterday and this afternoon we asked the minister to put these matters before the farmers before we committed ourselves to these principles.
The brief continues:
Yet, since the scheme proposed in Bill C-41 is a contributory plan, farmers should know what insurance they are buying; in other words, the plan must relate to the needs of individuals, and it should be possible for individuals to determine what benefits would accrue to them if the events against which they are insuring themselves should occur. That is a cardinal principle of all insurance plans-
That means individual responsibility for payments in and payments out. Does this bill provide for such a thing? The farmers want a scheme that is best for a whole area, not the fallacy which appears in the PFAA legislation which caused us so much trouble.
I should like to quote another paragraph from the brief as follows:
A second cardinal principle of all such schemes is that indemnities are paid to those who experience the ill effects of the event against which the plan provides insurance, and not to others. The proposed Prairie Grain Stabilization Act sins against both these principles; in fact it completely ignores them.
I think you can see why we proposed that before this bill repeated the mistakes of the LIFT program and the mistakes of Mr. Bennett in 1932, farmers should have a chance to decide what they want. After all they are putting up the money. The government should have been flexible and allowed the amendment to pass this afternoon.
I had a series of other points which I do not have time to go into, Mr. Speaker. There is the need for a foundation under this incomes plan. We could have built it on top of crop insurance or on top of the Agricultural Stabilization Act. Either would have worked, but the crop insurance program would have been the most suitable. Income protection could have been put on top of it on an actuarial basis and an individual basis, and there would have been no need for a great bureaucracy.
Western Grain Stabilization
Some support has been voiced for a regional system. Believe me, Mr. Speaker, I know why the minister turned that down. It would not work, just as putting the whole area into one block will not work.
The government moved away from gross income to net income, but as cost it brought in a list of seven or eight items. One of the greatest costs in farming today is interest costs, followed by labour and management. It will be interesting to hear the government's reaction when farmers realize what is missing from the bill.
I have expressed my views about bureaucracy. We do not want any more in western Canada. We had it under the PFAA and the old PFRA, and got rid of it. The minister is trying to build a political machine, and so he wants to add this new bureaucracy under his control. We believe that the principles of this bill can be made simple and easy to administer. This type of legislation is necessary, but we have no confidence in the minister and would like to get him off the backs of the farmers. Let the farmers be consulted. Let them decide what the principles should be. Let them support, with confidence, the type of legislation which is so necessary today.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING THE STABILIZATION OF NET PROCEEDS FROM THE PRODUCTION AND SALE OF WESTERN GRAIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been waiting for several days for an opportunity to speak on this bill, which is very important to western Canada. Two years ago this party suggested a plan or tried to encourage the government to develop a plan for the protection of the western prairie grain producer. The proposals we put before the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) at that time would have supported agriculture in other parts of Canada as well.
It is a great obstacle to agricultural producers to have to deal with two ministers, neither of whom will act on good honest proposals submitted on their behalf. It is a great misfortune that the government has adopted this policy.
Two years ago we asked the Minister of Agriculture to adopt certain crop insurance policies which would set the pattern for the industry. Our proposals, if followed, would have obviated the necessity for further stabilization of the grains industry of western Canada, but the minister did not accept our suggestion and left the way open for the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang), minister in charge of the Wheat Board, to put his finger in the pie. That is why we are facing so many problems today. Actually, many of our problems flow from the inequities associated with those two ministers. I cannot differentiate between the two. They are responsible for several programs, including the ones coming under Bill C-19, Bill C-50 and Bill C-41. We also have our crop insurance program.
If these two ministers knew what they were doing they would bring in one or two programs which would stabilize the entire agricultural industry. Such programs would benefit all agricultural producers. The ministers have not done that. Apparently they cannot agree, and that is why we face difficulty in the agricultural sector of our economy.
Inequities associated with the administration of our grains business have necessitated the program which the minister has now brought forward under this bill. When

May 6, 1975
Western Grain Stabilization
the present session of parliament began one of the first difficulties with which we had to deal was that of the grain handlers' strike on the west coast. Three Canadians contributed materially to that problem, namely, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) and the minister in charge of the Wheat Board. The latter minister threw his weight, or authority, behind the Minister of Labour and behind the Prime Minister when the government tried to force grain companies on the west coast to accept a 61 per cent settlement. We, on my side of the House, said that such a settlement would set an inflationary pattern which would be unequalled in Canada's history, but the government would not listen. In no way would it pay attention to what we were saying.
I am glad to see the minister sitting in his seat. I hope he will listen to what we say. Allow me to quote from a speech I made in the debate just alluded to, and I am quoting from page 226 of Hansard for October 8, 1974. After quoting the minister's words at a Vancouver news conference on May 24, to the following effect:
The government will introduce legislation to approve contract recommendations by conciliator Dr. Perry as a binding collective agreement on the two parties.
I said:
On what advice or consideration was such a cowardly step based? I hope the hon. members opposite recognize the importance of the situation with which we are dealing. On July 18 the Minister of Labour reaffirmed the government's decision to force settlement terms upon the grain companies. The minister responsible for the Wheat Board urged producers to exert pressure on their own organizations in order that the inflationary conciliation recommendation would be accepted. What right did he have to do that? A telegram sent by the two ministers to the grain companies on August 23 reads in part:
'We have made it quite clear, as has the Prime Minister, that the
government will legislate the recommendations of Dr. Perry, if
necessary.'
Of course, that position met resistance. Why? Because the grain companies are owned by the producers and they backed the companies up to the hilt. Ninety per cent of them supported the companies. What else could they do? What else could the companies do, if they were to discharge their responsibility to those they served? Clearly, the three members of the government previously referred to have put the government into an intolerable position. Let me put on record letters which the companies have received from farmers.
I then read into the record the following letter from a farmer at Cupar, Saskatchewan:
Do I, as a grain farmer, also get a 61 per cent increase in the price of my products? In two years time can I negotiate as a body for another 60 per cent increase? ... I agree that when the cost of living increases 10 per cent, so should everything else-not 60 per cent. I, as a farmer, am finally able to get my head a little above water. If price and wages increase at the same rate, that water is going to get... deep again. Keep up the good work.
What I have just quoted shows why our agricultural economy is in difficulty. Government promises enabled the government, including the minister in charge of the Wheat Board and the Minister of Labour, to be elected in the July 8 election last year.
On April 8, as recorded at page 4599 of Hansard, I asked the Minister of Agriculture the following question:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Agriculture and arises because of his presence at the Rome food conference. As it takes about one month to load grain for Bangladesh on the cargo carrier Amoco Cairo, one of the largest vessels ever to enter the port of Vancouver, because it is necessary to tow the ship into ocean water several times during the loading and turn it around in order to keep

the cargo balanced, and as this ship must drop anchor 65 miles from the port of destination because of shallow waters, it is obvious somebody boobed. Can the minister advise the House who is responsible?
Neither the Minister of Agriculture nor the minister in charge of the Wheat Board rose off his posterior to answer. Then we were told the ship would carry 4.8 million bushels of grain and would take about one month to load, if there were no delays. I point out that there was a ship in Seattle harbour which would take on 4.2 million bushels of grain in five days, using seven men to load. Further, the ship carrying Canadian grain had to anchor 65 miles off-shore from Bangladesh; it could not unload nearer the coast because it could not go into shallow waters. I said, when I asked my original question, that somebody boobed. I suggest that repeated boobs on the part of the two ministers concerned are creating problems for agriculture.
This afternoon we voted on an amendment which was defeated. We asked the minister to allow us to take this bill out to the producers and give them some input as to the type of program they want. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) mentioned that the Manitoba crop insurance people were in town today appearing before the Senate Agricultural Committee. I know crop insurance commissions from other provinces are also appearing before that committee. I think it rather unfortunate that a request I made of the Standing Committee on Agriculture was refused when one of these commissions was in town. The request was refused primarily because the government will not listen to advice from my side of the House. Ministers go along in their own bull-headed way and will not listen to good counselling.
The hon. member for Bruce-Grey (Mr. Douglas) suggested that the committee is going to travel. Has the hon. member discussed the idea with the Minister of Agriculture and the minister in charge of the Wheat Board? Certainly I see no support evident on the part of the hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley (Mr. Mclsaac), or on the part of the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Goodale). They are so busy patting the minister on the back for what he has done that they are failing those who elected them by not criticizing the government for what it is doing. In no way will the people of those constituencies receive adequate representation until those two members adopt a different stance.
Let me quote part of the brief that the Manitoba Crop Insurance Commission presented earlier today to the agricultural committee of the other place. It says in part:
We suggest that the present all-risk crop insurance programs operative in the western provinces could be broadened to include price guarantees. Prices for the various crops could be adjusted from year to year to reflect changes in the cost of production and to protect profit margins so that net farm incomes would be kept commensurate with the general standard of living in Canada. By adding price guarantees to the present yield and quality guarantees of the crop insurance program, farmers could be offered a complete package of basic income protection.
The program could be operated by the crop insurance administration presently existing in the western provinces. With a slight addition to staff Manitoba Crop Insurance Corporation could administer a much more equitable crop and income insurance program than is envisaged in Bill C-41. It would also make it unnecessary to establish a complete new administrative organization to administer a separate western grain stabilization program.
May 6, 1975

Above all, the approach suggested by Manitoba Crop Insurance Corporation is consistent with the cardinal principles of mixed private and social insurance, that the insured knows what he is insured against and what his benefits will be, and that payments are not made at random but to those who need them.
This is the type of program we want to see put in place. It would have been so easy, but apparently the minister does not understand. He does not seem to understand that the Crop Insurance Commission presently establishes that there will be so many bushels of grain sold at so much a bushel. If you multiply those factors you arrive at an answer in dollars and cents.
It is ridiculous for the minister to tell the House there is a great difference between the two systems. The scheme proposed here is unnecessary, and it will cause many problems for grain producers. The minister's record has been poor. He has probably been one of the poorest ministers any government has had.
One of the first problems with which I had to deal as a member of parliament arose because of regulations and laws connected with the operations of the Wheat Board which were not working to the benefit of producers. The producers were caught. Everyone knows that when a permit book is taken out a producer may allocate so many acres for, malting barley. Perhaps the House will allow me to use barley as an example. As we all know, frost, rain, and weather conditions generally determine whether the barley will actually malt or not. In this instance frost hit the crop and producers could not deliver their grain as malting barley simply because it would not malt. Therefore the agent required a permit from the Wheat Board to transfer those designated acres back to allocated acres.
I made representations to the minister responsible for the Wheat Board, but he said he could do nothing. It would seem to me that, when producers are caught in this web of legislation passed by parliament, every effort should be made to help them, particularly by a minister in charge of the Wheat Board who is also Minister of Justice. Did this happen? No. They were hauled into court and had to pay fines of $50, as well as legal fees. The agent was fined between $200 and $300. This is not justice. We are not getting justice from the minister in charge of the Wheat Board.
Here we are asked to bring in another piece of legislation, and even the minister is not completely aware what the bill contains. Last night, when the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil) stated that an inventory would need to be taken at the end of the year, the minister said this was not the case. I will put this exchange on record.
