speechtext:
I appreciate, Mr. Speaker, that we are not supposed to deal with the bill in detail at this stage, but I should like to read just one excerpt because it does affect what we are discussing. This is from clause 9:
(4) For the purpose of determining the adjusted marketing to production ratio referred to in paragraph (1)(b) for a year under review, the Minister shall
(a) make the following calculation in respect of each of wheat, oats, barley, rye, flax seed and rapeseed:
(i)	divide the actual aggregate number of bushels of such grain produced in the designated area and sold by all producers in the year under review by the number of bushels per acre of such grain that is the average yield for such grain for the five years immediately preceding the year under review;
(ii)	divide the difference obtained by subtracting
(A) the opening inventory, in bushels, of farm stocks of such grain for the year under review, determined as being the closing inventory, in bushels, of farm stocks of such grain for the year immediately preceding the year under review, determined in December of that immediately preceding year.
The minister said it is not in the bill. He does not know what is in the bill. This is why the wheat producer is in such a horrible mess. If there were a business-like approach to the grain-handling system we could solve many of our problems, and there would be no need for programs like this intended to protect growers in years of hardship. What we are up against in Western Canada is the fact that labour leaders have been using the movement of grain as a whipping boy. The time is coming when we can no longer accept such a situation.
Every Canadian should be aware, too, that we depend to a great extent on grain exports to balance our foreign exchange account. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) has told us that our balance of payments deficit will be in the neighbourhood of $4 billion to $5 billion this year, and I can tell the House why this is so. Primarily it is because we had a poor grain crop in western Canada last year. I should like to put on record figures showing movement of grain in western Canada over a six month period in the last five crop years. In 1971 there were 330.2 million bushels; in 1972, 386.6 million bushels; in 1973, 410.8 million bushels; in 1974, 293.6 million bushels; in 1975, 275.1 million bushels. These figures are for clearance of grain for six month periods during those years, and the figures show a decline in the years 1974 and 1975.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the lower price of grain at the present time is adding to the problems of the Canadian economy and our balance of payments deficit. According to a report that I received some time ago, no grain cars had

May 6, 1975
Western Grain Stabilization
been unloaded at the Pacific coast or Thunder Bay terminals since Monday, February 17. As I said a while ago, we are unable to get our grain moving. If the minister in charge of the Wheat Board, together with the Minister of Labour, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien), and the Prime Minister would sit down with representatives of labour and get an assurance that our grain will be moved, our economy would be in a much better position.
I should like to put on record a comment in a newsletter put out by the Palliser Wheat Growers' Association as follows:
The government of Canada seems incapable, for whatever reason, to control inflation. In the absence of government guidelines and programs to curb inflation, it is difficult to expect labour and management to exercise restraint in wage demands and company profits.
Out of this situation arises the immediate problem: the complete shutdown in the movement of grain. This is resulting in a shortage of feed and food supplies for our customers and, most damaging of all, the loss of confidence in Canada's future reliability as a supplier.
To the Canadian grains industry this could be a near-mortal blow; Japan is our Number One customer for rapeseed and our Number Two customer for wheat and barley.
It seems to me that the way that the prairie grain producer would manage the situation would be to see to it that the grain is moved. If he made a contract for delivery, he would ensure that the person making the purchase would receive the product on time.
In the minister's speech he gave figures showing payments that had been made between the years 1968 and 1971 to the producers, but one thing he did not say was that one-third of the money paid out was subscribed by the producers. He said the money was paid out of a subsidy fund, and true enough it was, but one third was put up by the producers, the other two thirds being put up by the taxpayers of Canada.
We are concerned to see that this money is spent to the best possible advantage, and at the present time there is no way we can be assured that money paid into the fund will be used to the benefit of the prairie grain producer. It is a well known fact that any money returned to the producer will go to those in a strong financial position as well as to those who are not, something we ran into under the old PFAA. While that program was in effect one of its shortcomings was that money was paid out to those who did not need it as well as to those who did, and quite often some of the farmers who required money were overlooked.
I think it is unfortunate that the minister has more or less copied the old PFAA program, as well as incorporating into the new program the shortcomings of PFAA. I can think of farmers in any one of the three prairie provinces, as well as in the Peace River block in British Columbia, who could be completely wiped out because prices as well as production are up in other parts of the country; hence there would be no pay out. Producers may have to rely on this program to carry them over difficult periods, whereas we could have had an adequate crop insurance scheme for those who really require it.
If the minister had tied this program to a crop insurance plan, the extra money could have put in place a program that would not only have been acceptable to the producers but would have worked to their advantage. As it is we have no guarantee that the minister's present program

will work. Most of the crop insurance commissions in the four western provinces-I include British Columbia since it has a crop insurance commission too-fear that this program will have an adverse effect on their programs. I know the minister says these are two separate programs, and that one is complementary to the other, but things do not turn out that way, Mr. Speaker. People get fed up with this type of program. They may take one or the other, but I question whether they will take both in many cases.
When representatives of the Palliser Wheat Growers' Association appeared before the agriculture committee they told the committee that they were relying, and had relied, on crop insurance to get them over a bad spot. Now, in order to build up his ego, the minister is bringing in a program that could almost destroy the crop insurance scheme if the producers elect to participate in this new program and not crop insurance. If the producers do not accept both schemes, then actually one will work against the other. This is why the two schemes should be tied together. It is also why the crop insurance commissions are very pleased to have the opportunity of appearing before the Senate committee on agriculture.
I have felt that perhaps not too much good has come out of the Senate, but I hope that the Senate committee on agriculture will take a good look at this program before approving it. If, in their wisdom, they see it is not going to serve the purpose intended, then I hope they will turn it down. The vote we had this afternoon is an indication that the members on this side of the House do not have the manpower to turn it down.
I hope that our Standing Committee on Agriculture will have an opportunity of visiting the west and discussing this bill with the producers, individual farmers, and farm organizations, and that we will be able to put into effect a program that will benefit them. Certainly this is a grave responsibility, because the minute this program is implemented without any changes I would question whether it will serve the purposes the minister would like it to serve. I think he would like to put a program in place to do the job, but for the life of me I cannot see why he will not accept some advice in the development of a program that will work.
I see no reason in the world why the committee should not go out and discuss this matter with the farmers, and then decide what type of program is required. Let me impress upon the House, Mr. Speaker, that whatever program is set up it will be the only one, because there is not room for another. There is certainly no room for any more programs, and I would hope that this one will be designed so that it will serve the best interests of the producers.
I have a copy of a letter written by the Flax Growers of western Canada to the minister in which it is stated:
We would respectfully request that you use your best influence to assure that the Standing Committee on Agriculture hold public hearings in Western Canada on Bill C-41.
We believe that our members would gain a much better understanding of this bill and the mechanics of operation of the proposed stabilization plan, through discussion at a public meeting, than is possible from its perusal.
May 6, 1975

The subject is too important to be left to representatives of organizations alone. It would also be impossible for our members to make representation in Ottawa in any numbers.
Our association will present a brief on this bill to the standing committee and would appreciate the opportunity for discussion of its contents.
Surely the minister will grant this request because the agricultural community is going through a very serious period in its history. Grain has been dropping in price in the last six months. It would appear that western Canada at the present time is about a month late with seeding, and we are not sure just what kind of crop we are going to get this year. If we have an early frost, as we did last year, the crop could be as short as it was then.
In addition, there are increased costs of production. Fertilizers are up 50 per cent, including ammonia and 11:48. We were told the other day that as of July 1 freight rates are going up 25 per cent to the chemical industry. The minister was out west and flew a kite when suggesting that perhaps we could take another look at Crowsnest Pass freight rates. I believe he was in Edmonton when he said that. I think he was flying a kite, and he found out that western grain producers soon shot it down. He has been trying to retract the statement ever since. Just the other day I noticed a statement from the minister's Regina office which said that he was not going to touch those rates. If he was not planning to touch them, why did he mention this? He certainly frightened the very dickens out of the western grain producers when he mentioned that. They guard these rates very jealously because they know that if they are changed the cost of grain movement will quadruple over a 12-month period.
I have been asked many questions about this bill, and I should like to refer to one query by an officer of a grain company who is also a producer. He stated in his letter:
The plan is described as voluntary, which is some stretch of the imagination.
Farmers near retirement will not join the plan because they could not withdraw their contributions a few years later when leaving the farm.
Should feed mills receive financial consideration for the extra book work involved?
This is a very important point. I said earlier that this minister caused me problems when I first came to this House. I saw innocent producers and grain handlers fined in our courts, and there was nothing I could do. The minister in charge of the Wheat Board in his dual capacity as Minister of Justice told me there was nothing he could do either.
We are now getting involved in the same sort of thing, but it is even worse. There is a penalty section in this bill which provides for a fine of up to $5,000 for an infraction. These grain dealers are supposed to deduct the 2 per cent representing the producer payments and forward them to the stabilization account within 30 days. What happens in the fall of the year when these grain handlers or elevator operators are handling a great deal of grain, are very busy and go over the 30 days? According to the law that will be legislated by this bill if it is not changed, they will be liable to a charge and a fine in our courts of up to $5,000.
What happens to feed mill operators if they should happen to do the same thing? The minister has suggested that there can be the movement of grain through licensed
Western Grain Stabilization
grain dealers. What about the grain that is transferred from one farm to another? Is that to be included under this bill? What happens in respect of the grain sold by one farmer to another? I do not think there is any provision in the bill for that.
What this is going to mean is simply that if producers take part in the program the farmers will haul their grain and sell it to the feed mill operator, who will in turn sell it to the feeder. There will be extra charges and extra costs involved, which means less profit for the producer and for the feedlot operator.
There are so many faults and holes in this bill it is as the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) has suggested, just like a sieve.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset of my comments I want to re-affirm the commitment of the New Democratic Party to the principle of income stabilization for farmers. Indeed our party has been the pioneer of orderly marketing systems and price supports that would guarantee Canadian farmers a decent livelihood and would ensure the viability or rural communities. To those goals we remain firmly committed. We will continue to expose and oppose, with all the force and determination that we can muster, any attempt by the government to destroy the system of orderly marketing of western grains through the Wheat Board, and any attempt to force western producers back on to the mercy of the open or so-called free market.
It is perfectly understandable that members of the New Democratic Party are suspicious of the moves that are made by the Liberals in respect of western grains. Over the last few months we have been witnessing their attempts to weaken the authority of the Canadian Wheat Board by turning domestic feed grains back to the Winnipeg Commodity Exchange.
We have been hearing proposals for the repeal of the Crowsnest rates, to which the preceding speaker for the Conservative Party quite correctly alluded. We have been hearing calls for the abandonment of thousands of miles of branch lines on the prairies. We have also seen amendments introduced to the Agricultural Stabilization Act which is now in committee, which make specific provision for the support of wheat, oats and barley grown on the prairies and marketed, not through the Wheat Board as they should be, but on the open or so-called free market.

Now, following an abortive attempt to foist an unacceptable stabilization bill on western farmers in 1971, an attempt that was stopped by the combined opposition of every farm organization and every provincial government involved, as well as by the determined efforts of the NDP members in this House, we have another stabilization bill that is simply too complex, too complicated, and too inexplicable. Several of my colleagues at earlier stages in this debate outlined our objections in detail to the bill so I shall be brief, much to the relief of some of my urban colleagues to my right.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING THE STABILIZATION OF NET PROCEEDS FROM THE PRODUCTION AND SALE OF WESTERN GRAIN
speechtext: No. I want to hear you.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING THE STABILIZATION OF NET PROCEEDS FROM THE PRODUCTION AND SALE OF WESTERN GRAIN
speechtext:
I was very sorry that the amendment proposed by the Conservative Party this afternoon was voted down. I think it would have been most appropriate to refer the subject matter of this bill to a committee of the House before proceeding further. I agree with them on that point. Not only would this have permitted some clarification of the principles behind this particular scheme, it would also have afforded an opportunity to canvass, in co-operation with farm groups, other possible kinds of stabilization plans. I think that should be done.
I should like to summarize briefly some of the problems in respect of this particular piece of legislation. We will do our best to deal with these in the form of amendments at the committee stage. The purpose of this legislation, briefly stated, is the continued operation of a free market in western grains and the need to protect producers from its inevitable failings. Production surpluses and deficits will continue to exist after the passage of this measure. Under this bill the government is to play no active role in determining the allocation of productive resources. In our view this is a fundamental fault.
The stabilization effect of the plan is reduced by a number of factors, and I shall single out a few. We are in a period of decline. The five-year average of net cash flow would become progressively lower. Net income would show a progressive decline. Producers would continue to contribute the levy. Pay-outs would occur during periods of relatively high but falling commodity prices, whereas no pay-out would occur during periods of relatively low but rising price levels. The cost of the plan to the federal government is overstated, and the stabilization effect reduced due to the fact that a portion of federal contributions, around 15 per cent, would be recovered through taxation when a payment is made.
Because the stabilized margin or net cash flow is not indexed to inflation, net income would decline in terms of real dollars at a rate approximately equal to the rate of inflation, with no support payments being made. Stabilization payments themselves are not included as proceeds in calculating the five-year average. Further, the levy is based on the financial position of the stabilization fund, not on ability to pay. The levy could actually increase in a bad year. Surely this is an undesirable situation.
Finally, the support level drops to 90 per cent of the five-year average after the fund has been in a deficit position for three years. What are the implications of aggregate calculations and pay-outs? Because the plan operates on an aggregate basis, all regions and all grains are lumped together in the calculation of aggregate pay-
May 6, 1975

outs. This offers little or no protection on a regional or commodity basis. For example, rapeseed producers may experience depressed markets but not receive any payouts from the plan if the aggregate proceeds from all grains-and wheat of course is dominant-remain at or above the five-year average level.
Eligible expenses incurred in the production and sale of grain include only cash expenses as listed in the bill. They exclude depreciation on buildings and machinery, interest on indebtedness, interest on equity, and the labour and management of the producer himself. Surely this is another undesirable feature of this measure.
An individual producer's share of the aggregate pay-out, in a year when a stabilization payment is made, is determined in proportion to his share of contributions through levies for that year and the immediately preceding two years. In other words a producer who has had good sales, and therefore has made a relatively substantial contribution to the fund, will receive a proportionately high payout. A producer who has done less well will receive proportionately less. The plan therefore rewards good fortune, and penalizes misfortune. He who needs most gets least.
At this point I would like to refer to an important point that was made before the Senate committee on agriculture this afternoon by the deputy minister of agriculture for the province of Manitoba in a discussion of this bill. He compared some of the provisions of this bill with what exists in our unemployment insurance legislation. It reads:
If the Unemployment Insurance Commission operated on the same principle as the grain stabilization plan, it would calculate for all of Canada the average annual bill for wages and salaries on which unemployment insurance contributions are made, adjust it for changes in the number of unemployment insurance contributors and for certain changes in the consumer price index, and if the adjusted total wage bill fell below the average of the previous five years, the Unemployment Insurance Commission would make a payment to all wage and salary earners. Each would be paid proportionate to his contributions; those who had paid the maximum would receive most; those who had paid less would receive less, and the unemployed who had made little or no contributions would receive little or nothing.
I know that such a scheme to stabilize the net proceeds from wages and salaries in Canada would be rejected not only by the ordinary working people in Oshawa but by the working people in every village, town and city across Canada. Yet such is the principle at the heart of the bill.
I believe that all Canadians, consumers as well as producers, whether they live in cities or rural areas, have come to see the urgency of providing adequate and stable incomes for our farmers. I think also that most people can understand the need to support the farming industry as a whole, just as our society now supports, through a variety of means, almost every industry in one way or the other by way of sharing in a variety of governmental schemes. What we must insist upon, however, whether in respect of industrial subsidies or support for agricultural producers, is some assurance that the funds so used will be used to achieve their desired effect. It is in this respect that my colleagues and I object most seriously to a number of details in this bill, although there is over-all agreement on the basic principle.
Wheat Payments
It is concern with these detailed objections that will lead members of my party to present to the House and to the government amendments at committee stage, and we hope at that point that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) will show more wisdom and flexibility than he has up to this point in the debate on this very important subject.

subtopic: TWO-PRICE WHEAT ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR PAYMENTS FOR WHEAT PRODUCED AND SOLD IN CANADA FOR HUMAN CONSUMPTION
speechtext:
That Bill C-19, an act to provide for payments in respect of wheat produced and sold in Canada for human consumption in Canada, be amended by deleting "1980" in lines 27 and 32 at page 2 and substituting therefor "1977".
He said: Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in the debate on Bill C-19, and on the motion which I put forward, I should like to point out that this debate is taking place at a very unsettled time with regard to the world food situation.
I am one of those who, over the years, have been deeply concerned about people throughout the world starving, and I was particularly pleased and proud that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), who was at the Rome food conference in late 1974, vouched for the Canadian contribution to alleviate the plight of starving people throughout the world. I was disappointed at that time that the United States, a much wealthier country than ours, a country much more capable of producing food for human

May 6, 1975
Wheat Payments
consumption than is Canada, was so reticent in offering its resources to satisfy the hungry world.
Having said all that, I now come to Bill C-19, an act to provide for payments in respect of wheat produced and sold in Canada. The concept of Bill C-19 is basically that world wheat demand and world wheat prices will rise, but wheat sold to Canadian millers will sell at $3.25 a bushel. Any amount of money above $5 a bushel, at which world wheat sells, will be compensated by the producers, and any amount of money between $3.25 and $5 will be compensated by the government.
This is a very interesting piece of legislation at a time when world food supplies are, I repeat, in what might be called an unsettled condition, a thunderstorm, a reoccuring storm, or what might be called at best stormy conditions. We saw world wheat prices rise well above $6 a bushel in December 1974. In early 1975 we witnessed the withdrawal by the USSR of its offer to purchase wheat from the United States. This caused world wheat prices to drop from January 1 until the middle of April by about $2 a bushel. The interesting thing is that throughout that drop no comparable drop took place within Canada. Wheat prices within Canada dropped from about $5.90 per bushel on the international market to $5.16 at Thunder Bay on April 1, the asking price of the Canadian Wheat Board. The reason I point this out is that it must obviously be clear to everyone that the Canadian wheat farmer is still subsidizing wheat later by the Canadian consumer.
This bill locks the wheat producer into a seven year agreement. I cannot overemphasize that. Everyone in this House has witnessed several labour negotiations. I can recite the railway negotiations, the longshoremen on the west coast, grain handlers and longshoremen on the St. Lawrence, and so on. None of them relate to a seven year contract. Bill C-19 locks wheat producers into a seven year contract. What has this parliament got against wheat producers? Why lock them into a fixed price for their commodity?
We all know that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) is unable to control inflation, much as we might wish he could. We might admire his command of the finance portfolio, but we know that he cannot contain inflation within Canada because he does not have the support of the Liberal party or of the Liberal cabinet in his back pocket. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) runs this country, and the Minister of Finance is just one of those people who must grapple with the facts. Grappling with the facts does not enable him to reach the proper conclusion with regard to inflation. We have come to the conclusion that inflation will continue, whether we like it or not.
Bill C-19 locks Canadian wheat producers into a seven year agreement which suggests that Canadian millers will buy wheat for $3.25 a bushel, and the government shall make up the difference between $3.25 and $5. On anything over $5 the poor-I cannot overemphasize that word- producers must bear the loss. When this bill was studied in committee, we were told that all farm organizations agreed with it. But before I get to the committee question, I should emphasize what my amendment does. It proposes

to delete 1980 in lines 27 and 32 on page 2 and substituting the year 1977.
In other words I am saying that we should stick with $3.25 and a subsidy up to $5 until the year 1977. That is a two year contract. Is it so unusual for this House to be asked to support a two year contract? What labour and management negotiations has this House dealt with in recent years? It has dealt with the railways, the grain handlers on the west coast, grain handlers on the St. Lawrence river, and all of them in two year contracts. Why should we superimpose our desire for a seven year contract upon the farmers? Do we think farmers are so naive that they will willingly negotiate this contract? Do we think farmers are so ignorant that they do not know the facts?

HEALTH-IMMIGRANT MEDICAL STUDENTS-REQUEST FOR DATA ON WILLINGNESS TO SERVE IN GENERAL PRACTICE AND IN REMOTE AREAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, tonight I am going to speak in the adjournment debate on the question of bringing foreign doctors into Canada when we have many fully qualified medical students who are being rejected by our universities. One student was even rejected because he was one point too low in mathematics.
It is incredibly selfish for us to bring in half our supply of doctors in the provinces from less affluent countries. Is that Christian ethics, or is it foreign aid in reverse? One doctor came from a country which only had one doctor for every 5,000 people. We have one doctor for every 700
5540
i

May 6, 1975
Adjournment Debate
people. Many of those doctors could not qualify for our Canadian medical schools because their education was held to be inadequate. We are concerned about our medical manpower, but where is it? Are the medical authorities concerned about this, or are they shelving their responsibilities? Is medical manpower receiving attention at the federal level?
The only criterion for entrance to Canada is that a doctor wishing to come here must practise where a doctor is needed. That is the admission ticket, and that is some ticket. If a foreign doctor comes to this country and goes to some remote area, he may find it cold, or develop arthritis. He will be lonely and upset, and may develop emotional difficulties and go to the city. Of course if he is in B.C. he can go to Vancouver or Victoria and enjoy a fairly warm climate.
To say that escalating health care costs and abuses can be cut by cutting the number of doctors in practice is nonsense, is pure rubbish. People want to see a doctor; they do not care how many doctors are on the street; they only want to see one. A health care program, if honestly handled, would in no way increase health care costs. It always amuses me to hear people say, "We are well fixed for doctors; we have one for every 620 or so." Let us look at the figures.
About half our doctors are specialists and only see referred patients. What about the othef half? Many of those doctors have administrative jobs. They work as insurance medical examiners. They do part-time work. They include members of parliament. Others do local parttime work only when they feel like it. Some work short hours, and only in hospitals. So really, how many doctors are there in general practice? Is there one doctor to every
2,000	people?
In addition, of course, you must consider those who are teachers and researchers. Their numbers must be subtracted from the total. Anyone who argues that health care costs will not go up must, of course, show the government how to take care of all the old people who become ill as they go over the hill in their 40s, 50s, 60s and 70s. As people get older they tend to develop more and more diseases, and you see multiple diseases developing in the same person. We are training geriatricians. Western University, at London, Ontario, I believe has a qualified geriatrician as head of that university's intended chair of geriatrics. Queen's is making a start in this field. Actually, Western had to go outside Canada to obtain a qualified geriatrician.
Let's consider the list of applicants. The University of Toronto leads in having the most medical freshmen born outside this country. I understand that 25 per cent of their freshmen class were born outside Canada. But we reject hundreds of Canadian boys and girls who were born in Canada, who have been brought up in our customs and know our reactions. Many of them have a burning desire to minister to the sick. Many have compassion and feel the urge to become involved in this field. When rejected by this country and its institutions, they go to Ireland, Mexico, or other countries, and come back, after taking this circuitous route, to practise in Canada.

You know, it has never been proven that brilliant students make better doctors. Often the bright and the brilliant suffer from offsetting disadvantages. Often the average student with average marks makes the best doctor.

subtopic: HEALTH-IMMIGRANT MEDICAL STUDENTS-REQUEST FOR DATA ON WILLINGNESS TO SERVE IN GENERAL PRACTICE AND IN REMOTE AREAS

subtopic: HEALTH-IMMIGRANT MEDICAL STUDENTS-REQUEST FOR DATA ON WILLINGNESS TO SERVE IN GENERAL PRACTICE AND IN REMOTE AREAS
speechtext:
All of us in the profession can point to examples showing the truth of what I say. After all, what have mathematics, physics and chemistry to do with general practice?
In conclusion, we say we need foreign doctors to go to our wide open spaces. I object to this tactic. We are asking those doctors to go to places where our own, native trained doctors will not go. How wise are we? I suggest that we shall often find that these foreign doctors will practise for a little while, but then become sick. It is cold in outlying parts, and they are not used to those conditions. They develop arthritis; they get emotionally ill, so they head for the big cities.
Wouldn't it be far better when the prospective medical student is filling out his application for entrance to the university, to ask him: are you willing to go into general practice in outlying areas or where required for the next three to five years? Give him incentives to do that- remove his income tax. You would then find you would be able to pick the number of doctors who would go there, and they would be all the better doctors because of their training in that field. I ask the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) to accept his responsibility in the medical manpower field, to admit some of these average students of medicine, and to stop discrimination against students who may be, in the long run, the best general practitioners of all.

subtopic: NATIONAL PARKS-RIDEAU-TRENT CANALS- AUTHORIZATION OF TOLLS-ESTIMATE OF REVENUE

speakeroldname: Mr. A. D. Alkenbrack (Frontenac-Lennox and Addington):
subtopic: NATIONAL PARKS-RIDEAU-TRENT CANALS- AUTHORIZATION OF TOLLS-ESTIMATE OF REVENUE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my subject of debate at this time on the
May 6, 1975

adjourned motion is one of vital interest to the tourist industry of southern Ontario in the region traversed by the Rideau-Trent canal systems. Up until this year, 1975, these systems have historically remained, as they should always be, free of tolls. Their construction is unique in the western hemisphere and a marvel of construction methods of the 19th century, especially in the Rideau system where the name of Colonel John By, its builder, will endure for centuries.
These canal systems have drawn an increasingly important patronage to the tourist industry, not only from our own users, but all over the North American continent, and a healthy and prosperous tourist industry has been built up along these waterways. This industry has helped our balance of trade more and more each year, and no impediment should be placed in its way. But now the government, through the Ministry of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, has announced that it is placing toll and lock charges on these waterways. I must protest this action as strongly as possible.
I first brought this matter to the attention of the minister in the form of a question on March 24. A supplementary question yielded the information from the minister that the expected revenue would be more than $11 million. He did not give me the right answer to my question. I was asking how much revenue they expected to receive from the canal systems. His answer of $11.6 million was the expected revenue from the whole parks system. I have learned since that they only expect about $300,000 per year revenue from users of the canals, Mr. Speaker. This sum is not worth the effort and should not be levied, considering the damage it is going to do our tourist industry and outfitters along the canals.
I have always been among those who advocate as much freedom as possible in our roads, waterways and communications systems. That is why I have always fought the increase in tolls on the St. Lawrence Seaway just as I fight the installation of tolls and lock charges on the Rideau-Trent tonight. The government is apparently seeking to Americanize our free systems and, in doing so, to stultify and discourage private business. These two waterways have been the vehicle which has helped build our tourist industry and brought business to tourist operators. These operators in turn, individually and collectively, pay tremendous amounts of taxes, municipal, provincial and federal.
I brought this matter up the other night in committee, in fact on April 24. I stated there, and I state again, that the action of the government in placing tolls and lock charges on these formerly free systems directly promotes inflation. By placing charges and tolls on publicly owned and free waterways, the government in a sense is saying, "We are going to get ours-our revenue" and is saying to the tourist operator, "You get yours the best way you know how".
The natural result of this move by the government is to reduce patronage of the waterways by the Canadian and American public, and at the same time reduce patronage and use of the tourist hotels, outfitters and tourist businesses all along the waterways, including the sale of fuel,
Adjournment Debate
licences, fishing tackle, liquor, beer, meals, marina services, room and motel and hotel accommodation, and everything that is required for holidayers and tourists. The reduction of gross business may necessitate the raising of rates for accommodation. This is inflationary.
The government already has a taxation stake and interest in those other revenues, so in imposing tolls for the comparatively paltry sum of an estimated $300,000 the government is only going to cut off its nose in order to spite its face. If the government has any regard for the people of southern Ontario who depend on the tourist industry for a living, it should forget about this installation of tolls.
I am not alone in my fight. The hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) has protested this, as has the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Cossitt) and the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Rynard). Here is a recent report from the Ottawa Journal of April 30 headlined "Lock tolls will hurt tourism":
A federal government plan to charge lockage fees on the Rideau Lakes waterway has drawn sharp criticism from resort and marina operations and the boating public.
Regulations now being drafted by the Department of Indian and Northern Affairs (which administers Parks Canada) would have pleasure craft under 18 feet paying from $3 a day to $50 a season to use the locks. Craft more than 18 feet would pay from $4 to $80.
It's the first time in 70 years that tolls will be charged. And businessmen along the waterway are worried.
"It's bound to affect that tourist trade," said Roy Towle, president of the Smiths Falls Chamber of Commerce. "When people add up the cost of boats, campsites, gasoline and now this, they just won't come."
Joseph Kenny who runs a hotel at Jones Falls, near Elgin, Ontario, is worried his business will drop this summer and he's been writing to his regular guests urging them to protest to Ottawa.
Mr. Kenny's hotel at Jones Falls is typically one of hundreds of small businesses to be unfairly and adversely effected by this toll and lock charge policy.
There is also another point, Mr. Speaker. There is more than the tourist industry involved here. The government is discriminating against the local farmers, landowners, residents and cottage owners along the canal systems who have always used their historic right freely to use the waterways. Farmers often have to go up or down through a set of locks to tend their cattle or livestock, to cut wood, or practise forestry in the husbandry of land, and indeed often have to go through a set of locks to go fishing. Cottage owners often have to go through a set of locks to go to the nearest village to buy their provisions.
These people have riparian rights that the government is now going to charge them to use. If the government insists on putting tolls in place Mr. Speaker, it should give the people I have mentioned special free permits to use the locks; but I protest, as strongly as it is physically possible for me to do so, the charging of tolls to anyone.
On behalf of those in business and resident along the Rideau-Trent waterways from Ottawa to Kingston and from Trenton to Georgian Bay, I call upon the government and its ministry of Indian and northern affairs to reconsider this ill-advised scheme which will be so harmful to these residents, to the tourist industry, to the province of Ontario and to Canada as a whole, and to maintain the free use of these waterways by the already heavily taxed public.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-NAMIBIA-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO PREVENT FALCONBRIDGE MINES FROM EXPLOITING WORKERS AND END PRIVILEGE OF CLAIMING FOREIGN TAX CREDITS
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-NAMIBIA-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO PREVENT FALCONBRIDGE MINES FROM EXPLOITING WORKERS AND END PRIVILEGE OF CLAIMING FOREIGN TAX CREDITS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Namibia, formerly Southwest Africa, was assigned to the Dominion of South Africa by the League of Nations to be held in trust; with a mandate to guide that territory toward political modernity and economic development. For nearly 50 years South Africa neglected her responsibilities and treated Namibia as a colony of her own. For years, as she does today, South Africa refused to co-operate with international organizations, arguing that the United Nations did not have authority over a territory assigned to her by the League of Nations, a different

organization, all the time exploiting the resources of Namibia, which rightly belonged to the Namibian people.
Finally on October 27, 1966, the General Assembly of the United Nations took decisive action by terminating the South African mandate and declaring the area to be under the direct responsibility of the United Nations itself. That was United Nations Resolution 2143 (XXI) of 1966.
In July, 1970, the Security Council called upon all states in Resolution 276:
-to withhold from their nationals or companies of their nationality not under direct government control, government loans, credit guarantees and other forms of financial support that would be used to facilitate trade or commerce with Namibia-
In addition the council asked states:
-to discourage their nationals or companies of their nationality not under direct government control from investing or obtaining concessions in Namibia and to this end withhold protection of such investments against claims of a future lawful government of Namibia.
The issue has become increasingly more important. The International Court of Justice in a recent ruling regarding South Africa's presence in Namibia stated:
-that a binding determination made by a competent organ of the United Nations to the effect that a situation is illegal cannot be without consequence-the precise determination of what is to be done is a matter which lies within the competence of the appropriate organs of the United Nations.
This is a specific reminder to countries like Canada of their obligations to uphold Security Council resolutions dealing with Namibia.
Finally the United Nations Commissioner for Namibia issued a decree on the natural resources of Namibia, which has as its purpose the outlawing of any extractive industry in Namibia which operates without the permission of the United Nations Council for Namibia.
It was this kind of background which led me to place some eight questions on the order paper to probe the extent of Canadian involvement in Namibia. These questions led to the discovery that Canadian based corporations operating in Namibia can claim a foreign tax credit under Section 126 of the Income Tax Act.
The largest of these corporations is Falconbridge Nickel Mines Ltd. which shares ownership, 75 per cent to 25 per cent, with the Industrial Development Corporation of South Africa in Oamites Mining Company Ltd.
Falconbridge's performance in Namibia is not one we should be proud of; contract labour, poor housing conditions for black workers, vastly inferior wages and benefits for black workers, and no job advancement for Namibians. Through it all our Canadian government is calmly studying it all, and studying, and studying, and waiting for this report and that report.
It seems to me that this situation is quite clear cut. Canada has agreed by its vote at the United Nations that the government of South Africa is an illegal authority in Namibia. It is not right that Canadians should seek economic gain there in ways which, directly and indirectly, involve an acceptance of such an authority.
How much more reprehensible it is for the Canadian Government to go on making all sorts of fatuous state-
May 6, 1975

ments about helping developing countries achieve economic stability and health! How gross it is for our Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to be talking about a new economic world order which would give citizens of third world producer countries a better deal! How phoney! The only ones getting a better deal in the Namibian experience are the shareholders of Falconbridge Nickel Mines, and the bosses of South Africa. And don't forget, Mr. Speaker, that even more despicable is the fact that Falconbridge is extracting non-renewable resources from Namibian lands and seas, so that when South Africa finally decides to turn Namibia over to United Nations trusteeship, and eventually to SWAPO, there will be few, if any, resources left.
I would urge the government to initiate the following action now: First, to inform Canadian-based companies that Canada recognizes, as the only legal authority in Namibia, the United Nations Council for Namibia. This position is totally supported by the International Court of Justice, the Security Council and the General Assembly of the United Nations and our vote in that body. Second, since the only legal authority is the United Nations Council for Namibia, henceforth no Canadian-based corporation in Namibia will be permitted to claim foreign tax credits for income taxes, fees, royalties and other payments where such were paid to the Government of South Africa. Third, the Canadian government instructs all Canadian based corporations to negotiate any exploitation or concessions of Namibian resources with the only legal authority there, namely, the United Nations Council for Namibia. Fourth, all Canadian-based operations in Namibia must be informed of these decisions.
That is the kind of action that is needed. Is the Acting Prime Minister trying to tell this House that a government which was as tough as it was in 1970 bringing in the War Measures Act to crush a handful of dissidents, lacks the courage to live up to our international commitments? Who is the Acting Prime Minister afraid of? Was he afraid of world opinion when he supported the United Nations' free Namibia? Is he afraid today to tell Falconbridge Nickel Mines that he supports that position? I don't think he is afraid. I just think he and his government are mealy-mouthed. We have seen that in the so-called energy crisis, the Chilean fiasco, and the recent stranding of approved South Vietnamese immigrants to Canada. Truly it may be said of the Acting Prime Minister and his government as it was said of the seventeenth century Spanish viceroys in New Spain, "They obeyed all laws, but enforced none".

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-NAMIBIA-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO PREVENT FALCONBRIDGE MINES FROM EXPLOITING WORKERS AND END PRIVILEGE OF CLAIMING FOREIGN TAX CREDITS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I
Adjournment Debate
wish to respond on behalf of the Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Breau).
The Department of External Affairs, in consultation with other interested departments, has for some time now been examining the question of Canadian companies operating in Namibia. Under Canadian law the government cannot force a mode of conduct on business operations of subsidiaries of Canadian corporations in Namibia. It is, furthermore, a principle of government policy not to interfere in the operations of Canadian companies abroad. The various Security Council resolutions on Namibia, and the General Assembly resolutions of 1967, are not mandatory resolutions under Chapter VII of the UN Charter and do not, therefore, impose binding obligations on member states, as is the case with regard to Rhodesia.
The government's position on Namibia has been outlined publicly several times, at the UN and in other international bodies. While we have articulated it in response to inquiries from individuals and companies, it may be appropriate and useful for us to repeat it here. Canada does not recognize the right of the Republic of South Africa to legislate in or for Namibia. In 1971 we informed the government of South Africa that Canada accepted the advisory opinion of the International Court of Justice to the effect that South Africa's administration of Namibia was illegal.
However, we must recognize that South Africa does de facto remain in control of Namibia. But, as I indicated, the Government of Canada does not recognize this as having a legal basis. The Canadian government recognizes that the Council for Namibia has the right to make decrees concerning Namibia that are within its competence. The applicability of such decrees, their effectiveness and their status, however, must be examined individually and are dependent upon further action that the United Nations may take either through the General Assembly or the Security Council.
The Canadian government considers that any Canadian companies operating in Namibia do so entirely at their own risk and initiative. Should such companies be subject to confiscation or nationalization of their properties in Namibia, the government's attitude will accord with this position.
